World.title: Why are there suddenly so many data centres planned in Canada? Your questions answered
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This story idea came from audience members, like you, who got in touch with us. Send us all of your questions about data centres and the environment. We are listening: ask@cbc.ca

In 2026, AI seems to be everywhere — and some Canadians are questioning whether they want the massive buildings that power it humming away in their backyards.

Canada has bet big on AI, and part of that push is a boom in planned or proposed AI data centres, which require vast amounts of water and energy.

Proponents say the facilities could help secure Canada's future as an AI leader. But the rapid pace of development has some communities hitting pause. In Ontario, Oakville voted in August to impose a one-year moratorium on data centre construction, while Mississauga is set to vote in September on a similar moratorium. Councillors there brought forward the motion after a data centre the size of three football fields was proposed.

On Thursday and Friday, hundreds of people turned up at town halls to demand answers from Alberta's technology minister over the province's plans for AI data centres.

People rally before participating in a march to protest the opening of AI data centres, in Vancouver, in June. Telus is moving forward with two new AI data centres in Vancouver and the expansion of an existing facility in Kamloops. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Many CBC readers have also reached out with questions about the sudden spike in data centres being built in Canada.

Here's what we know.

What are data centres?

A data centre is a facility that houses and powers computer servers, networking equipment and other technology needed for computing and storing data. Any time we visit a website or watch a movie online, a physical server processes that request for us.

But the AI data centres making headlines today are much larger and more energy-intensive than traditional data centres. They use more powerful computer chips — graphic processing units, or GPUs — driving up energy consumption and requiring more intensive cooling systems to manage the resulting heat.

"For an older style conventional cloud facility, we might have a couple of megawatts moving into that building, but for AI facilities, it's much more common to see hundreds of megawatts," Anne Pasek, Canada Research Chair in Media, Culture and the Environment at Trent University, told CBC News.

These facilities can span thousands of square feet, with "hyperscale" data centres becoming more common. Definitions of hyperscale vary: some place the threshold at 50 megawatts, others at 100. Just 50 megawatts is enough electricity to power 37,500 homes.

Aerial images show construction of the TOR1X0 Data Centre at SteelesTech Campus in Toronto. The three-storey data centre and office building, designed by WZMH for Yondr Group, is southwest of the intersection of Steeles and Victoria Park avenues. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

"The facilities we're building for AI are just bigger and bigger, both in terms of the footprint that they have in the lands they occupy, in terms of the energy bills and water impacts that potentially come with them," Pasek said.

Why are so many being built in Canada suddenly?

Demand for AI has skyrocketed in recent years, and Canada is looking to establish itself as a leader in the field, hoping to attract investors and give the economy a boost.

In 2024, up to $700 million was dedicated specifically to leveraging investments in new or expanded data centres.

Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled Canada's national AI strategy in June , dubbed "AI for All," promising at least $2 billion in new investments. One stated goal is to increase AI adoption among Canadian businesses from 12 per cent today to 60 per cent by 2034.

WATCH | Carney unveils national AI strategy: Carney's AI strategy big on jobs and training promises, light on details | Duration 1:57 Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled the government's long-delayed strategy on artificial intelligence, pledging 250,000 AI-related jobs and billions for training programs, but little in the way of privacy and safety details.

Supporters say wider AI adoption is inevitable and Canada is better off staying ahead than being left behind.

"It's a facet of modern life," Martin Karsten, a professor of computer science at the University of Waterloo, told CBC News Kitchener-Waterloo on Aug. 18. "As long as we are all very interested in using these [AI] services, I think we have to accept the fact that these data centres keep coming."

But many communities are pushing back, citing concerns about water, energy and health. Critics also question whether data centres bring enough local economic benefits to offset those concerns, saying they provide a temporary boost in construction jobs but do little to spur secondary industries.

Some experts have warned that the rush to fund AI could be a bubble that could burst, potentially leaving AI data centres as stranded assets. Some companies that embraced AI are now pulling back in the face of rising costs , raising questions about the technology's return on investment.

Canada currently has only five hyperscale data centres with a capacity of at least 50 megawatts, but 159 facilities were proposed or under construction across the country as of July, according to a recent York University study . Of those, 116 are expected to have a capacity of more than 100 megawatt capacity — a first in Canada.

The study found the scale of the industry is ramping up rapidly. Over 200 new projects have been announced, with an average capacity of 122 megawatts — more than ten times the average capacity of Canada's 194 active sites.

While most active data centres are in Ontario, followed by Quebec and British Columbia respectively, the majority of proposed projects are in Alberta. If all are built, Alberta's share of total data centre capacity in Canada would rise from three per cent to 93 per cent.

"If you look at the location of the data centres, we can see that the amount of electricity that the average new data center would use is as much as some of the communities where they're going to be located in," Alexander Carlo, a postdoctoral researcher at York University's Schulich School of Business and one of the study's authors, told CBC News.

Data centres accounted for 4.4 per cent of U.S. electricity demand in 2023, according to the U.S. Department of Energy, which predicts this share could rise as high as 12 per cent by 2028.

During a heat wave or snowstorm, electrical grids may struggle to handle the added load from a data centre, Pasek said, increasing the risk of brownouts. There are also concerns that the additional strain could increase consumers' power bills .

WATCH | Digging into the hyperscale data boom in Canada: A hyperscale AI data centre boom is coming | Duration 6:21 A boom in hyperscale AI data centres in Canada is coming, promising economic opportunity and tech sovereignty, but as CBC’s Nora Young explains, there’s a growing resistance to the impact the massive, power-hungry facilities have on local communities.

How do data centres affect water sources?

Computing equipment generates a lot of heat, so facilities use water to cool it. Many cooling systems then evaporate that water to expel the heat, meaning it may not return to the water cycle in the same place.

"They can pull water from a watershed, that water can evaporate off, become a cloud, that cloud will float away, and will become rain in a totally different region where that water doesn't get returned to the [original region's] watershed," Pasek said.

Smaller-scale operations can draw tens of thousands of litres a day, while hyperscale operations can draw more than a million.

A 2025 report by the U.K. Government Digital Sustainability Alliance found that a single 100-megawatt hyperscale facility could consume about 2.5 billion litres of water annually — enough to serve 80,000 people.

Some areas can absorb that demand, but in a drought-stricken regions, it could pose a problem.

"We are already water bankrupt in many places around the world. So adding an extra pressure on the system, even if it's small, can have significant impacts," Kaveh Madani, director of the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health, told CBC News in August.

WATCH | Why data centre communities worry about water: Why data centre communities worry about water | Duration 6:02 As resistance to AI data centres grows, industry leaders say there are ways to build more community-friendly facilities. For Radio-Canada, Anaïs Elboujdaïni examines the water concerns and explores the arguments for a more sustainable approach in Canada.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said in August that the province's data centre framework would prioritize closed-loop cooling systems, which reuse water and cut down on intake compared to evaporative systems.

Are there health risks with living near data centres?

Experts say there can be, but the risks vary depending on the data centre's size, design and power source, meaning that different data centres can carry vastly different risks.

Air pollution

Data centres can draw electricity from local grids, but it can take years to fully connect them. As a result, many are now being designed with on-site power plants fuelled by natural gas or methane gas. When powered by fossil fuels, data centres produce emissions that contribute to climate change as well as a type of air pollution called fine particulate matter, also known as PM2.5.

Wildfire smoke is one of the main sources of PM2.5, a dangerous type of air pollution. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

"We do know that exposure to fine particulate matter increases the risk of all kinds of [negative] health outcomes, from respiratory, cardiovascular and neurocognitive," Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard Chan School of Public Health, told CBC News. She added that chronic exposure to air pollution can also increase annual hospital visits and worsen asthma.

An independent analysis she worked on with EmPower Analytics Group examined a specific AI data centre steps from a residential area in Northern Virginia and found its eight natural gas turbines and 51 diesel generators could result in $53 million to $99 million US a year in health-related damages.

Studies have suggested that chronic exposure to PM2.5 may also be linked to a higher risk of lung cancer.

Noise pollution

Like other industrial buildings, data centres produce noise around the clock from fans and backup diesel generators. They can also emit a low-frequency hum, and chronic exposure can cause stress, sleep problems and long-term health complications, Dominici said.

According to NBC News, residents have filed at least 15 lawsuits in 12 U.S. states over constant data centre noise in the past three years.

WATCH | Toronto residents pushing back on data centres: Why these Toronto councillors, residents are pushing back against data centres | Duration 2:13 Some Toronto councillors and residents are pushing back against two proposed data centre projects in Etobicoke and Scarborough. As CBC's Naama Weingarten explains, they are concerned about potential noise, electricity demand and water use.

Concerns have also been raised that closed-loop cooling systems could affect water quality if wastewater is mismanaged. Much remains unknown about the overall risks, Dominici said, which is why she believes development should be paused to give researchers more time.

"There has been a race to build these AI hyperscalers without really thinking through about what could potentially be the negative health impact on the surrounding community," Dominici said.

Are there alternatives to traditional big-box data centers?

Experts say it's a question of trade-offs. One option is to make data centres more sustainable.

The health risks associated with air pollution, for example, can be mitigated if a data centre and its backup power systems use wind and solar instead of fossil fuels.

"If you could make the facilities optimally efficient and power them with renewable energy, either in the moment or stored in batteries or other types of storage, we'd be making some real progress there," Daniel Bresette, president of the U.S.-based Environmental and Energy Study Institute, told CBC News.

But that approach is more expensive, meaning developers may have little incentive to adopt it without regulations or community pressure. Most new projects in Alberta are set to use natural gas, including a $13-billion AI data centre project announced by Meta last month.

The facility, shown in this rendering, will be a one-gigawatt, nearly 270,000-square-metre data centre powered by a natural gas-fired plant. Meta, the tech giant behind Facebook and Instagram, says it's building a new AI date centre in Sturgeon County, Alta. (Handout - Sturgeon Data Centre/The Canadian Press)

Reducing noise pollution through design can also be costly. Some regions in the U.S. are introducing zoning restrictions based on noise pollution and requiring developers to conduct noise studies before construction.

Locating AI data centres in more remote areas can also reduce risks to the general population, but it could shift those impacts onto rural and Indigenous communities.

A proposed $70-billion gas-powered data centre in northern Alberta is currently being challenged by nearby Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation, which says it was not properly consulted about a water license.

WATCH | UN report investigates environmental risk of AI data centres: UN report highlights environmental impacts of AI data centres | Duration 1:39 The United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health has released a report that examines the environmental impacts of AI data centres. It comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled his new AI strategy that includes plans for 'large-scale' data centres throughout the country.

Another option is to spread AI computing capacity more broadly rather than hyperscaling it, Pasek said, in order to "break up the burden" on communities.

The third option is to "rethink fundamentally what we want AI to be," she said. This could mean a return to smaller, open-source development rather than massive AI projects that, in her view, are profitable only if the technology is pushed onto businesses and Canadians.

World.title: 'Super' El Niño didn't cause this year's fires and heat waves, but it's about to take us on a 'wild ride'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Whether you call it a "super" El Niño or a "Godzilla" El Niño, the Pacific Ocean warming event that disrupts global weather patterns is back and packing a punch, at a time when many parts of the planet are already overheated.

This July was the hottest on record for North America and Europe, where successive heat waves have led to thousands of heat-related deaths, dried up rivers and fire-scorched landscapes. That includes Canada, which has already seen more than 4.1 million hectares of woodland go up in flames and produce thick smoke that blanketed much of the eastern half of the country and parts of the northern U.S.

Although this scorching summer aligned with the arrival of an El Niño and climate scientists say it's not to blame for those devastating extreme weather events. However, they note we may only be starting to see how this naturally occurring phenomenon could amplify extreme weather already super-charged by fossil-fuel driven climate change.

"El Niño's impacts are going to be large and broad across a huge area," said Josh Willis, a climate scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

"Get ready, because it's going to be a wild ride."

WATCH | What might happen when El Niño mixes with human-caused climate change: El Niño expected to add fuel to climate disasters | Duration 2:06 The UN's weather agency is warning that the return of El Niño will make temperatures even higher this summer, which they also warn will exacerbate climate disasters, including drought and wildfires.

Flipping the weather upside down

El Niños occur naturally every three to seven years, usually beginning in spring and enduring well into the following year, as the water surface temperature in the area of the Pacific where they form along the equator, rises at least 0.5 C above the average.

Willis says that warming heats up the air above the water and "rearranges the atmosphere."

"It flips the weather upside down," he said, causing drier places to get heavier rainfall and wetter regions to dry up.

A satellite map from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration shows sea surface temperature anomalies recorded on Aug. 20, with hotter than average temperatures stretching across the El Niño region toward the west coast of South America. (NOAA)

Although this El Niño may have begun forming in May and June just as successive heat waves and fires began to scorch the northern hemisphere, Willis says they usually don't start to impact northern places like Canada until they peak in the late fall and winter.

But Muhammad Azhar Ehsan, a scientist at the Center for Climate Systems Research (CCSR) at New York's Columbia University, says this El Niño is so unprecedented that while he can't directly link it to current heat and wildfire conditions, he does wonder if the "exceptional" temperatures associated with it could be contributing to these disasters.

At the very least, he thinks it's grounds for more research

Ehsen says this El Niño is on track to rival those experienced in 2015-16 and 1997-98, the strongest El Niños since official records began in 1950.

WATCH | How a very strong El Niño will affect the planet in 2026 and into next year: What exactly is a ‘super’ El Niño? And what does it mean for you? | Duration 3:25 Some climate models predict 2026 will be an El Niño year — and that it'll be a particularly strong one. CBC’s Nick Logan breaks down what that means, and what Canadians can expect.

What to expect when you're expecting El Niño

Models suggest much of Canada and the northern U.S. can expect a warmer winter than usual due to this El Niño, with British Columbia's normally wet south coast potentially seeing far less precipitation and a much lower snowpack.

The southern U.S., meanwhile, is likely to experience a much wetter winter.

There are also noticeable effects happening right now in the tropics that Willis says are likely associated with El Niño. He says the phenomenon "sort of juices up" conditions that may already be occuring.

Peru and Ecuador sit at the eastern edge of the El Niño region, where Willis says a lot of warm water has "smashed up" against the coast, posing a threat to fisheries.

Peru is also bracing for heavy rains and flooding in some areas and drought in many inland regions.

"But we're also beginning to see a lot of drought away from the equator," Willis said, highlighting a prolonged lack of rainfall in Panama, which is already affecting water levels in the lake that supplies the Panama Canal.

At the opposite end of the El Niño region are countries like Indonesia, which is already experiencing a much longer and more active wildfire season.

16-year-old Rudiyansah wears a Superman costume while extinguishing a fire at a wildfire-affected area in Indonesia's Central Kalimantan province on Aug. 14. (Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana/Reuters)

One thing people in North America can see happening now, Willis says, is the change to the hurricane season. In an El Niño year, there are fewer tropical storms and hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean.

"The jet stream, which is migrating a little bit farther south, tends to shear off the top of the hurricanes in the Atlantic," he said.

"And because we have all this warm water in the Eastern Pacific, it fuels storm generation there and tropical storms and depressions, which might not have been hurricanes otherwise."

The Eastern Pacific season has already recorded nine named storms ahead of peak season — including Category 5 Hurricane Genevieve in late July and Lala, which caused significant damage as a tropical storm on Hawaii's Big Island last week.

WATCH | Hawaii's Big Island spared direct hit from Lala but suffers widespread damage: Tropical Storm Lala leaves destruction across Hawaii | Duration 1:40 Despite not making a direct hit, Tropical Storm Lala left widespread destruction on Hawaii's Big Island. Lala was downgraded from hurricane status on Sunday morning, but forecasters warned it remained powerful and dangerous

An El Niño born into a much warmer world

The record heat and wildfires this summer were the result of human-caused climate change, which has already been attributed for the past four years being the hottest on record, says Zachary Labe, climate scientist at U.S.-based nonprofit organization Climate Central.

"El Niño is just sort of a temporary boost on top of this long-term trend," Labe said.

But such a significant warming event happening in a world that's even hotter due to climate change could, he says, defy expectations climate scientists have based on previous data.

Authorities in Panama have begun restricting shipping through the Panama Canal, seen in this March 13 file photo, as the country copes with drought conditions exacerbated by El Niño. (Enea Lebrun/Reuters)

Labe says what's more certain is that we'll be dealing with the effects of this El Niño well into 2027.

"Because it takes time for that El Niño to have all that heat that's building up in the ocean to transfer into the atmosphere," he said.

"So, this will be around with us for at least the next six to 12 months."

World.title: Canada's an agricultural superpower. Could it feed the whole world?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On a Tuesday morning in Coleville, Sask., Dean Roberts watched as a large grey drone whizzed up into the air and flew around his 4,000-hectare farm, which produces an array of crops including canola, wheat, barley and lentils.

He was getting a demonstration of the DJI T100, currently the largest available spray drone in Canada. It sports a 100-litre tank that can be filled with pesticides to spray onto crops — a practice the federal government approved in June .

For the demonstration, the equipment dealers filled the drone tank with water. As it zipped around the fields, Roberts explained how this technology could make a difference to his farm's operations.

"The lentils like a drier climate," Roberts told CBC's The House. "So in our area when we get very wet, we have to apply a fungicide to keep the leaf disease pressure down until the crop reaches maturity.

"One of the challenges is, our ground rig often can't drive across the field when it's that wet. So this drone could be an option for us."

Roberts places a battery inside the spray drone he's considering for his farm. He has used drones in the past to locate rocks that can cause expensive damage to his other equipment, but a recent federal policy decision now allows him to use drones to apply specific pesticides on crops. (Emma Godmere/CBC)

The drone, Roberts added, is the next iteration of the sort of technological adaptation that Prairie farmers like him have been making for generations, all in the service of increasing their crop output.

But when it comes to the adoption of agricultural technology, Canada is lagging behind other countries, Roberts said. The U.S., China, Brazil, Japan and Australia are well ahead of Canada in allowing drone spraying.

"Drones existed, we could physically buy them, but we didn't have a regulatory environment to actually use them [to spray pesticides]. So in this case I would say regulatory holdup was our delay here," Roberts explained.

Experts count red tape, infrastructure bottlenecks and labour shortages among the factors undermining Canada's ability to send more food around the world, while competing countries continue to scale up their exports.

WATCH | Regulation change brings renewed interest in pesticide-spraying drones: Regulation change brings renewed interest in pesticide-spraying drones | Duration 1:52 Health Canada lifted its restrictions to allow drones to spray pesticides at the end of June. Since then, dealers and farmers say there's been a surge of interest in the technology.

According to the federal government, Canada exports about $100 billion worth of agri-food products annually, but the rate of growth is not keeping pace with other nations.

"Essentially, the total size of the pie of global food trade has grown faster than Canada has grown," said Evan Fraser, executive director of the Arrell Food Institute at the University of Guelph. "We are producing less in terms of the overall percentage."

According to an RBC analysis from February 2025, Canada had slipped from fifth to seventh on the global food export leaderboard — overtaken by China and Brazil — and could fall to ninth over the next decade.

The RBC analysis also said Canada's market share since 2000 has declined by 12 per cent. Though the country's food exports have still quadrupled in that time, the analysis noted the rest of the world's exports have grown five-fold.

Fraser said that Canada has a reputation for having a very slow policy and regulatory framework that leads to slower uptake by farmers of new technologies and agricultural products.

However, he acknowledged that the same framework means Canadian food "is among the highest quality, most trusted and safest in the world."

Roberts said there's not a single solution to this issue, but rather several small aspects that need to be improved. He highlighted some positive signs, such as Canada rebranding its pesticide regulator , which he hopes will improve timelines around crop protection products and approvals.

"But again, this is still new as well," he said. "We need to see it on the ground here at the farm gate."

Infrastructure and labour challenges

Even if he can get access to the latest technologies to bolster his farm output, Roberts said he faces another big challenge: getting his crops to global markets.

"The vast, vast majority of our crop is going to go to export, and for my farm where I sit, there is only one viable way to get it to tidewater, and that is the railways," Roberts said. "The average western Canadian crop has 1,500 kilometres of rail line to tidewater."

But those railways are subject to all sorts of delays, like bad weather in the mountains or on Canada's West Coast, Roberts added. If that happens, fewer rail cars can operate, which backs up the grain elevators where he deposits his time-sensitive crops.

Rail cars are seen on the tracks outside the Viterra Cascadia Terminal that handles grain exports in Vancouver on July 12, 2023. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

"And when there's one week of delays at the railways, it can take weeks once service resumes to resolve the bottleneck because the system is generally running fairly full," Roberts said. "I can't drive my truck 1,500 kilometres to Vancouver to dump at the port."

Evan Shout, co-founder and CEO of Maverick Ag, an agriculture business consulting and risk management firm in Saskatoon, concurred with Roberts and said infrastructure concerns often come up when he coaches other farmers.

"Those infrastructure issues that are real issues come to the forefront when you're the last person to get paid," said Shout, who's also CFO of Hebert Grain Ventures, one of the largest farms in Saskatchewan.

"It's one of those uncontrollable risks," he added. "We don't control the trade partners our government works with. We don't control the investment into infrastructure. We don't control when they load what boats."

Roberts and Shout also highlighted issues with finding enough workers to harvest crops, since farming can be a very challenging profession with seasonal work schedules.

Evan Shout is the co-founder and CEO of Maverick Ag, an agriculture business consulting and risk management firm in Saskatoon, and the CFO of Hebert Grain Ventures, one of the largest farms in Saskatchewan. (Emma Godmere/CBC)

"We're very busy in seeding, harvest and spraying over the summer months. When guys want to be at the lake, farmers usually aren't," Shout said. "And then all of a sudden we get into winter and it's a little slower. So how do you get somebody that's used to that seasonality?"

Roberts said farming equipment has also become more complex, meaning operators need to be highly skilled.

"You can't just find anybody off the street to run it anymore. You have to have a certain tech background. You have to have a certain mechanical inclination to fix it, work on it," Roberts said.

To raise these issues, Shout stressed the importance of having a seat at the table with federal decision makers, and added that while advocates exist, he feels they are often relegated to the "secondary table."

WATCH | Potential fast-tracking of Port of Vancouver expansion worries environmental groups: Potential fast-tracking of Port of Vancouver expansion worries environmental groups | Duration 2:02 A plan to expand the Port of Vancouver has been sent to the federal major projects office, and could be declared a project of national significance. As the CBC's Katie DeRosa reports, the move comes amid a push for economic diversity and concerns about the environment.

"I think part of it is, we need to be seen as what we're actually providing to Canada," Shout said, adding that it's beneficial for Canada's food security to have farmers involved in key conversations.

"If we don't produce strong food, we don't have the ability to send it to other countries," he said.

Agriculture Minister Heath MacDonald said in a statement to CBC News that the federal government is "tackling obstacles that hold our farmers back and creating new opportunities for Canadian agri-food exports."

MacDonald said Ottawa is investing in critical infrastructure projects through the Trade Diversification Corridors Fund and assisting the Vancouver Gateway Strategy, which is now with the Major Projects Office.

"Our government remains committed to reducing barriers to trade, strengthening our supply chains, and ensuring Canadian businesses can thrive both at home and around the world," MacDonald said.

Is boosting exports the right goal?

The federal government's national food security strategy includes several initiatives such as red tape reduction and billions of dollars to scale up Canada's domestic food production. The strategy is focused on bringing down the cost of food for Canadians, but it also references boosting export capacity.

Jennifer Clapp, a professor and Canada Research Chair in the School of Environment, Resources and Sustainability at the University of Waterloo, said it's a compelling goal but needs to be thought through carefully — and that may be easier said than done.

Clapp said rather than simply trying to boost its exports, Canada can refashion itself as a "sustainable agricultural powerhouse" and help other countries improve their own domestic capacity through eco-friendly agriculture.

WATCH | Carney announces $3B food security strategy: Carney announces $3B food security strategy | Duration 1:28 Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a new $3-billion national food security strategy to combat issues in the Canadian food system in Toronto on Thursday.

She added that if Canada pursues new markets for its crops, it may run into roadblocks since other countries are also pursuing greater agricultural self-sufficiency.

"I think we shouldn't necessarily be encouraging other countries to also become reliant on imports if we're not trying to do that," Clapp said. "It's a little bit contradictory."

"Also, there's risks for other countries because if we're dumping our products on poor countries, that could undercut the ability of their small-scale producers to have a livelihood," Clapp added.

Fraser said Canada should prepare itself to be a more important agricultural power, since modelling he's done has found climate change will make Canada more productive while reducing the output of other countries, especially those near the equator.

WATCH | Canadian farmers reel from trade disputes, geopolitical tensions: Canadian farmers reel from trade disputes, geopolitical tensions | Duration 2:07 Canadian farmers say ongoing trade disputes with the U.S. and supply-chain disruptions caused by the Strait of Hormuz closure are taking a toll on their bottom line.

"I think we should be preparing ourselves as a country for the future where we become a more important breadbasket," Fraser said. "I think saying no isn't appropriate because it's going to happen, given the nature of the changes we're facing."

Asked whether he thinks it's possible for Canada to feed the world, Roberts said the country has lots of arable land and a great climate for farming.

"So absolutely, we can feed a lot of the world. I don't know about the entire world with one province, but we can take a shot at it."

World.title: B.C. family feels 'violated' after burglary during wildfire evacuation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When the threat of wildfire dissipated and people could return home, a family in Summerland B.C., was shocked to find their house in shambles.

Their house was not destroyed by the Bald Range wildfire, as they feared.

Instead, Mira Boucher says her home was ransacked by looters while her community was empty and vulnerable — with every single house vacant under the evacuation order.

"Unfortunately, when we opened the front door, and the kids rushed in, someone had clearly been through the house," said Boucher.

"The kids are doing their best, but it's very traumatic. Especially after the trauma that preceded that with the wildfire evacuation," she added.

Small valuables, like computers, jewlery and gaming consoles were stolen from a home in Summerland while its residents were under evacuation order for a wildfire. (Submitted by Mira Boucher)

She and her family had only just moved into their house in Summerland a few weeks before the Bald Range wildfire sparked, and many of their belongings were still in boxes.

From their balcony on Aug. 7, the Boucher family watched flames crest the nearby mountain before grabbing what they could and leaving.

She said they had to flee quickly, in the middle of the night, with almost no notice.

"Just the clothes on your back, and a bag with some essentials," she said.

Boucher said after spending weeks on Vancouver Island while their community was placed under an evacuation order, her kids were eager to return home and see their rooms and belongings again.

Mira and Carl Boucher and their children had only moved into their home on an acreage in Summerland a few weeks before the evacuation orders were implemented. (Benoît Ferradini/Radio-Canada)

"When we got to the bedrooms, you could see everything, every closet and dresser had been flipped out, thrown on the beds, thrown on the floor. They were looking for valuables anywhere that we might have stored them," said Boucher.

"And then it just got worse and worse."

A door had been pried open and and small items including Boucher's jewelry, piggy banks, gaming setups and sports gear were taken. (Benoît Ferradini/Radio Canada)

A door had been pried open, and small items including her kids’ piggy banks, gaming setups and sports gear were taken.

Her jewelry and computer — along with that of her husband Carl — were stolen, and personal documents like birth certificates were also gone.

"We were violated in the place that was supposed to be the safest," Boucher said, adding that before bed every night, her children have been asking if they are safe.

WATCH | RCMP looking into cause of Bald Range fire: B.C. RCMP investigating cause of explosive Bald Range wildfire | Duration 2:57

Boucher suspects her family’s larger valuables, like bikes, were left behind because they could not be carried out undetected by thieves without a car.

She also says their treed acreage was targeted because it is more secluded than that of their neighbours, and may have been less likely to be noticed by RCMP patrol cars.

Only reported instance of burglary: RCMP

The RCMP said the Boucher’s home, located on a five-acre (two-hectare) orchard, is the only reported instance of break-in and theft from the time of the Summerland wildfire evacuation orders.

Officers were patrolling near more than 5,000 empty homes in Summerland for two weeks while the evacuation orders were in place, according to police.

Barricades, monitored around the clock by security and police officers, had been set up all around the community, preventing vehicle entry.

Police are now working with the Bouchers to recover what was lost. Recently, they were able to share some positive news with the family.

"They found lots of our personal items — birth certificates, IDs, various business-related papers — in a wagon near the trestles bridge," said Carl.

He added that the RCMP may also have also found clues, pointing them in the direction of where the rest of their belongings may have been taken.

The investigation is still underway, and the Boucher family is now working to rebuild, settle back into their home and overcome what they describe as a creepy feeling — of knowing someone entered your home and rifled through all of your belongings without consent.

World.title: Why do Canadians call the last letter of the alphabet zed?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If one thing binds us together as Canadians, it’s how invested we are in being different from Americans.

Few things distinguish us from our neighbours to the south more quickly than calling the last letter of the alphabet zed instead of zee, but why do we do it?

Though zed may feel quintessentially British, the word probably entered English from French .

When the French-speaking Normans conquered England at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, French became the language of the British court. For more than three centuries afterward , English kings grew up speaking French.

During that time, thousands of French words were introduced to the English language, including the French letter name zède, which was borrowed into English as zed.

Zed’s roots, though, date back even further — over 2,500 years to ancient Greek.

French inherited the word from Latin, its direct ancestor, which called zed by the similar-sounding name zeta. The Romans had picked up both the letter and the name zeta from the Greeks when they adopted the Greek alphabet to write Latin.

Zed is a descendent of Greek letter zeta. This twenty-sided die from the second or first century B.C.E. is inscribed with the letters of the Greek alphabet. (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

Zed remains the name for the letter not just in Canada and the United Kingdom but throughout the Commonwealth, in countries like Australia, South Africa and India.

That makes Americans the odd ones out when it comes to using the name zee, but they didn’t invent the word. It originated in Great Britain.

By the 1500s, a variety of alternate names for zed were in circulation in England, like zard, ezod, izzard, uzzard, and zee. Most of those pronunciations eventually died out, but zee was popular with spelling reformers , probably because it rhymed with other consonants like B, G and T.

One of the advocates for zee was Noah Webster, who published two groundbreaking American English dictionaries in the early 1800s. He popularized many of the spelling differences that distinguish American English from British English to this day, removing the u from colour, shortening tonne to ton and revising centre to center.

Webster’s motives weren’t just pedantic; they were patriotic . Calling himself “the prophet of language to the American people,” he saw his spelling updates as a way not only to align written English with American pronunciation, but also to assert America’s independence from its former English overlords.

“Customs, habits, and language, as well as government should be national,” he wrote in an essay published in 1789 . “America should have her own distinct from all the world. Such is the policy of other nations, and such must be our policy, before the states can be either independent or respectable.”

Noah Webster, one of the namesakes of the Merriam-Webster dictionary, was an American spelling reformer who promoted the name zee in the 18th and 19th centuries. (Library of Congress)

In his 1790 school speller and 1828 dictionary , Webster stipulated that Z should be pronounced zee. Much as contemporary Canadians use zed to separate themselves from Americans, he likely saw the letter as another way for Americans to differentiate themselves from their rivals, the British.

Webster’s spelling book was one of the first used in Canadian schools and — along with The ABC Song, copyrighted in Boston in 1835 — introduced zed to Canadian children, but there was pushback from British loyalists who felt Canadians should speak “the Queen’s English.”

An 1846 letter to the editor of the Kingston Herald complained that “the instructor of youth, who, when engaged in teaching the elements of the English language, direct them to call that letter ze, instead of zed, are teaching them error.”

The same year, Canada West (modern-day Ontario) adopted Irish National Readers as the standard textbook across its schools. The readers were written in British English and trained generations of Canadians to favour Britishisms like zed over Americanisms like zee.

Still, Canadian children haven’t escaped American influence.

We’re more inundated by U.S. media than ever before. For decades kids have been tuning into American educational programs like Sesame Street and Ms. Rachel that teach zee instead of zed, and it has influenced the way we speak.

In 1972, a study showed that up to 77 per cent of English-speaking Canadians said zed, not zee. Fifty years later, barely over half of Canadian adults have a firm preference for zed.

Affection for zed varies between the provinces. Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario, and Saskatchewan are zed strongholds, while zed is declining in the Maritimes, especially among younger age groups.

Perhaps surprisingly, since N.L. speech is often considered closest to British or Irish English, Newfoundlanders and Labradorians are the least likely of all Canadians to say zed.

Even in the 1970s, half of N.L. adults used zee over zed, and today Newfoundland and Labrador is the only province where the majority of people under 30 prefer zee.

That could be, in part, because teachers and books from the United States played a major role in the development of Newfoundland and Labrador’s schools and libraries in the 1800s and early 1900s, and textbooks weren’t standardized early on the way they were in central Canada.

It’s common to find what we would consider American spellings in N.L. newspapers from the nineteenth century.

The large American presence during World War II, when over 100,000 U.S. troops were stationed in St. John’s, Argentia, Gander, Stephenville and Goose Bay, may also have had an effect.

What’s perhaps most interesting is that as English-speaking Canadians get older they tend to ditch zee and start saying zed. If you ask a Canadian over 55 which they use now, they’re more likely to say zed than when they were in school.

That’s probably because for many of us zed really does become a marker of our cultural and national identity, a subtle way to distinguish ourselves as Canadian to anyone who’s listening.

World.title: Alberta premier urges return to trade talks, calls U.S. terms 'untenable'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith hopes federal negotiators will return to the table after the collapse of trade talks in Washington triggered a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian exports.

About $1.5 billion of Alberta’s $188 billion trade volume with the U.S. faces disruption, Smith said on her radio show Your Province, Your Premier Saturday morning. But she also said that the last minute demands from American negotiators were “untenable” and “too painful” for Canada to accept.

“I hope that they can get back to the table to negotiate something that’s more fair,” she said. “I’m really hopeful that some constructive conversations begin because, boy, the tariff war is painful.”

Smith spoke moments after Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada is imposing dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs on the United States starting Sept. 8. She said she hopes negotiations will resume, and a deal can be signed before that date.

Carney said during a press conference in Ottawa that American negotiators wanted to restrict Canada’s ability to sign trade deals with other countries. He also said the Canadian automotive industry would have suffered under the deal, and that there were objections to Canadian subsidies for French cultural programs.

"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said, adding that the United States “asked too much and offered too little.”

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette listen as Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks about Canada's response to new U.S. tariffs during a news conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Saturday, Aug. 22, 2026. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

Smith said she was surprised to hear about the proposed trade restrictions and said Alberta has been trying to double exports to countries outside the U.S.

However, she was cautious on retaliatory tariffs towards American goods, adding she has no interest in banning imports of U.S. alcohol. Alberta and Saskatchewan are the only provinces without a ban.

She also worried about the impact a trade war would have on farmers and agricultural equipment, and warned Alberta’s furniture makers and honey producers are particularly exposed.

“I know emotionally it feels good to retaliate, I get that. But…when retaliation happens, it means that everybody who is buying products from the United States are now going to face upwards of 50 per cent tariffs,” she said.

Smith will meet with her cabinet Tuesday to review the scope of the new trade measures, review federal relief proposals and discuss next steps.

Impacts to small businesses 'significant'

Alberta’s major exports of natural gas and oil won’t be impacted too severely by these latest tariffs, said Smith.

Kayode Southwood, a senior policy analyst for the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB), told CBC News on Saturday that small businesses across Canada and the province will still suffer “immediate and significant effects.”

Roughly 40 per cent of Alberta’s small businesses export to the U.S. and half import American goods, he noted.

“This round of tariffs is going to be much more impactful than previous rounds,” he said. “Any retaliatory tariffs that are applied by the Canadian government will hit those Alberta businesses hard.”

WATCH | Tariffs on Alberta businesses kick in after trade talks collapse: Tariffs on Alberta businesses kick in after trade talks collapse | Duration 2:21 Premier Danielle Smith says she’s urging the federal government to restart negotiations with the United States after trade talks fell apart late Friday night, bringing the Trump administration’s 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian exports into effect. As CBC's Jo Horwood reports, small business owners in Alberta are figuring out how to survive this trade dispute, while politicians and local business leaders consider whether walking away from negotiations was the right decision.

Calgary Chamber of Commerce president Deborah Yedlin told CBC News she supports Carney’s decision to end negotiations, but warned up to 100,000 jobs across Canada are vulnerable without a resolution.

She said she hopes both sides return to negotiations soon, but also framed the trade breakdown as an opportunity for Canada to re-evaluate its interprovincial commerce and expand its international trade relationships.

“We know that we have free trade agreements with 51 countries covering 60 per cent of the global GDP, but yet 33 per cent is what we’ve been exporting,” said Yedlin.

“We need to make sure that we make the most of those trade agreements, but at the same time it means that we have to really focus on building the infrastructure to get our goods to those new markets.”

World.title: Media concentration in Colombia
World.content:
Listen to this episode on Spotify

Colombia’s corporate media have played a dubious role in the history of the country and have concentrated an immense power for their owners.
