In 1994, he founded the liberal-democratic Reform Party and was elected to the Estonian parliament the following year, when he became foreign affairs minister.

Kallas was also an important figure in the Baltic country’s European trajectory: After his appointment as foreign minister, he oversaw Estonia’s bid to join the EU. He was prime minister in 2002, when the country concluded negotiations to become a member and was invited to join NATO.



“I think of courage required to rebuild a state and introduce its own currency in the early 1990s, as well as the quiet conviction he brought with him to Brussels,” wrote European Parliament Roberta Metsola on social media in response to the news. “Estonia and Europe are better because of his life’s work.”



“Through his public career, [Kallas] helped shape Estonia’s EU path and key European policies,” stated the Commission.

His daughter, Kaja Kallas, was Estonia’s youngest-ever serving prime minister, holding office from 2021 to 2024. She is now the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs for Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s second term.

This story has been updated.

World.title: ‘Shameful’: Israel faces international backlash after closing probe into Gaza aid strike
World.content:
Warsaw escalated the diplomatic pressure Thursday night by summoning Israel’s ambassador. Polish aid worker Damian Soból was among the seven people killed in the strike.

Poland’s foreign ministry said in a post on X that it “does not accept the perpetrators’ evasion of legal and moral responsibility” and stressed that prosecutors in Przemyśl are still looking into the matter. Warsaw also demanded Israel provide “all necessary clarifications and materials” requested by Polish investigators.

Israeli drones struck the World Central Kitchen convoy as it delivered food to civilians in Gaza, killing three Britons, an Australian, Soból, a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen and a Palestinian on April 1, 2024. The Israel Defense Forces described the attack at the time as a serious mistake and failure and pledged a thorough probe.

Closing the case this week, the IDF said it determined “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident.”

“Partnership requires mutual respect,” Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski wrote on X Thursday evening, warning that the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza and lack of accountability for the IDF’s “excessive use of force” were undermining public support “even in pro-Israel nations.”

World.title: From Middle East to e-sports: Macron hosts Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman
World.content:
French president Emmanuel Macron is on Sunday hosting Saudi Arabia's crown prince and de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman, for a two-day visit whose agenda ranges from e-sports to the war in the Middle East.

 

Several agreements covering health, transport and energy are to be signed on Monday, the second day of the visit, according to an official at the French presidency, underscoring the strength of relations between Paris and Riyadh. The leaders are expected to address the "major economic and strategic issues that underpin the Franco-Saudi partnership", the Élysée said, notably in energy, aerospace and defence.

According to the Élysée, the visit "reflects the vitality of the dialogue between the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and France, and will help to strengthen the strategic partnership that binds our two countries. To that end, the President of the Republic and the crown prince will for the first time hold a meeting of the Franco-Saudi Strategic Partnership Council".

The visit will, however, get under way on a different note on Sunday evening: Emmanuel Macron will receive Saudi Arabia's strongman - known as MBS from his initials - at the closing ceremony of the e-sports World Cup being held in Paris.

Still according to the presidency, "Organised for the first time outside Saudi Arabia since it was created, the staging of this global championship in Paris testifies to France's renewed appeal as a host for major international sporting events" and "also illustrates the shared ambition of France and Saudi Arabia to make sport and culture drivers of their rapprochement".

The event, which brings together the elite of e-sports - from video games to chess - and enjoys MBS's active backing, is being held outside Saudi Arabia for the first time.

The Élysée official declined to say whether the agreements might cover the large "Dragon Ball" theme-park project, backed by a Saudi fund and under consideration in Val-d'Oise, in the Paris region.

Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host a series of major global events, including the World Expo in 2030 and, above all, the 2034 football World Cup.

Will human rights be on the agenda?

Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States and historically at odds with Iran, is also closely following developments within the Islamic Republic in the wake of the US-Israeli conflict.

On Monday afternoon, MBS and Emmanuel Macron will chair the first meeting of the Franco-Saudi Strategic Partnership Council.

The two leaders "will exchange views on the main regional issues, in a context that calls for close coordination between France and its Gulf partners in favour of stability and peace in the Near and Middle East", to quote once again the Élysée's wording.

It remains to be seen whether human rights will feature prominently on the agenda, some eight years after the murder and dismemberment of Saudi dissident journalist Jamal Khashoggi inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018.

Related French judge opens probe into 2018 killing of Jamal Khashoggi

A United Nations investigation described Jamal Khashoggi's death as an "extrajudicial execution for which Saudi Arabia is responsible". US intelligence services concluded that MBS had "approved" the operation that led to Khashoggi's killing. Riyadh denies these accusations, blaming them on agents who acted on their own initiative.

In December 2021, Emmanuel Macron became one of the first Western leaders to meet MBS in Saudi Arabia after Khashoggi's killing. In July 2022 it was bin Salman who came to Paris - and that visit sparked fierce criticism on the left, Le Parisien (source in French) reported at the time. "On the dinner menu between Emmanuel Macron and 'MBS', the dismembered body of journalist [Jamal] Khashoggi ? (…) No ! Oil and arms !", the Green politician Yannick Jadot protested at the time. Julien Bayou, then national secretary of Europe Écologie-Les Verts, said in turn that "France is not a doormat for dictators in search of rehabilitation on the international stage".

Since then, the Saudi crown prince has made several trips to France: Saudi Arabia is too important economically and regionally for France to allow the relationship to deteriorate for long.

Ultimately, the oil factor - Riyadh is the world's leading crude exporter - especially against the backdrop of Russia's invasion of Ukraine and Europe's determination to wean itself off Kremlin fuels, has only served to seal this return to favour.

World.title: Raised in the wild: Spain's famous "wolf boy" dies
World.content:
Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja, Spain's famous "wolf boy", has, as has now emerged, died on Saturday 15 August at the age of 80.

 

Born in 1946 in a country that was just recovering from a civil war and a world war, Rodríguez initially grew up in the Andalusian village of Añora.

Rodríguez's life was marked by poverty, hunger and mistreatment. His father could barely feed the family, while his stepmother treated him brutally. When he was six, his father sold him to a goatherd, who left him in a remote valley where he was to herd livestock together with an old shepherd. The herdsman taught him how to survive in the mountains and use the resources available.

He hid from people

When the shepherd died shortly afterwards, Marcos was left to fend for himself. Over time he turned the wilderness into his home and found a family in the animals that surrounded him.

For twelve years Rodríguez lived a life without any human contact and developed his own forms of communication. He mastered the calls of the animals – from birdsong to the cry of the deer – and was convinced he could communicate effortlessly with foxes, wolves and even snakes. Throughout all those years he chose to stay far from civilisation and would run away or hide whenever he heard human voices in the mountains.

Rodríguez won the trust of a wolf pack when he fed its cubs and howled whenever he sensed danger.

The anthropologist Professor Gabriel Janer Manila carried out several months of interviews with Rodríguez as part of a social science study for the Faculty of Philosophy at the University of Palma de Mallorca. The interviews took place from November 1975 to April 1976.

Janer, the anthropologist, became a friend. In his view, Rodríguez was able to survive thanks to his intelligence and imagination. In his doctoral thesis Janer describes the different phases of Rodríguez's life: how he gradually became part of this community, how he learned its rules and the language of his surroundings, and how he treated the animals as equals.

"I cried and they jumped up onto me... then they showed me the way to their cave, the wolves' den," Rodríguez told Janer. He described how the wolf cubs played around him and leapt up at him as they greeted him.

Apparently, over time a kind of symbiosis emerged between him and the wolves.

"If I wanted fish, I went to the river and fished; if I wanted a rabbit, I caught one; if I wanted a deer, I called my parents, the wolves, let out a howl, hid in the river and the wolves drove the animals down to me," he said.

Janer later published his study in Spain as a book titled He jugado con lobos.

I was very well. I didn't know what money was, but I always had enough to eat. Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja

In 2010 a team from the TVE programme Informe Semanal spoke to Rodríguez in his home town Añora. At that point he was visiting the town for the first time in 60 years. Looking back on his time in the mountains, he told the camera: "I was very well. I didn't know what money was, but I always had enough to eat."

When he was discovered by the Guardia Civil in 1965 at the age of 19, he had to get used once again to life in human society: a difficult and lengthy process of adaptation. Rodríguez later stressed repeatedly that he had been happy in the mountains. His real suffering, he said, only began when he was found and forced to integrate into society.

Childlike naivety preserved

According to people who knew him, he seemed childlike in some ways, was "naive" about society and did not speak completely fluent Spanish.

He lived in Jaén with a priest, later in Madrid with nuns, did military service and eventually ended up in Mallorca, where he worked in hotels and restaurants.

After everything he had experienced in his life, Rodríguez decided to pass on his story – with the aim of "protecting nature and promoting a better understanding of it, because we have become so distanced from it".

He particularly wanted to convey this message to children: "Show more affection to your pets, because devices only need to be plugged in, but pets need love."

His life story was also brought to the big screen: "Wolfsbrüder" (original title: Entrelobos, German title: Wolfsbrüder) was released in Spain on 26 November 2010, and two years later, on 7 June 2012, the feature film was released in Germany.

Since 2001 Rodríguez had found a home in the village of Rante in the province of Ourense. The municipality of San Cibrao das Viñas, to which Rante belongs, said goodbye to its long-standing resident in moving words. "Marcos came to Rante with a story the whole world knew. He leaves behind a story that has become ours too," the municipality wrote on social media.

Rodríguez died during the festival held in honour of the municipality's patron saint.

World.title: French 2027 presidential election: Glucksmann to enter the race
World.content:
The former commentator turned politician, Raphaël Glucksmann, was due to announce on Sunday evening that he will run in next year's French presidential election, joining an already crowded field of contenders, including within the left itself.

 

At 46, this former essayist and MEP, who heads the centre-left party Place publique, was expected to make his bid official in a prime-time interview on the TF1 television channel.

It was also on TF1 that, on 26 May, the 46-year-old MEP announced that he was giving himself three months "to criss-cross the country", "to propose a new patriotic contract" and "to reunite his political family" ahead of the presidential election.

While the announcement comes as no surprise and will not change much in the short term, his decision is expected to have an immediate consequence: Glucksmann's partner, journalist Léa Salamé, a leading figure on rival public channel France 2, is expected to announce that she is stepping back to avoid any conflict of interest during the campaign.

The leader of France's far right, Marine Le Pen, sees her best chance yet of capturing the Élysée in 2027 after three failed attempts, but numerous candidates from President Emmanuel Macron's centrist camp (he cannot seek another term after two stints in the Élysée), as well as from the left, have already declared their intentions.

The leader of the radical left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is also running, for a fourth time, while the head of the Greens, Marine Tondelier, is campaigning in the joint primary despite being pregnant; former Green minister Delphine Batho has announced her candidacy to ward off what she calls a "rikikisation" and a "disappearance" of environmental politics; for their part, the Socialist Party (PS) first secretary Olivier Faure and even, potentially, former Socialist president François Hollande are considering throwing their hats into the ring.

In June 2026, Le Nouvel Obs counted more than twenty-five candidacies already officially declared or claimed.

Can "Glucksmania" cross the age barrier?

Opinion polls put Raphaël Glucksmann – popular among young people, to the point that some speak of a "Glucksmania" – on 10 to 12% of voting intentions; a respectable score, but probably not enough to reach the second round.

He can also point to his 13.8% in the last European elections, where he headed a PS-Place Publique list that made him the leading figure on the left.

In order to avoid an excessive fragmentation of the vote, the Socialist Party and Place publique plan to hold a primary in October to choose a single candidate. The details of this selection process are to be finalised in the coming days and approved by the bodies of both parties next Tuesday.

Rank-and-file Socialists, consulted in early July, rejected the open primary sought by PS leader Olivier Faure, opting instead for a "closed primary", reserved for members of the PS, Place publique or a "social-democratic pole", creating a smaller electorate more favourable to Raphaël Glucksmann.

Although Glucksmann strikes a more reformist and centrist tone than the PS, he has every interest in working with this historic party and drawing on its electoral machine, as he does not have a strong enough structure of his own to support his likely candidacy.

The son of philosopher André Glucksmann, he worked between 2009 and 2013, when he was still a young idealist with unruly hair, as an adviser to Mikheil Saakashvili, the staunchly pro-Western former Georgian president. Currently imprisoned in his home country, Saakashvili was a determined opponent of Russia after the 2008 war between the two countries.

A fervent defender of Europe and a fierce opponent of the far right, Glucksmann is also a vigorous supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion and is known for his hard line on Vladimir Putin's Russia.

Born in Beirut and aged 46, Salamé had already announced that she would step down from presenting the flagship news bulletin she has anchored since 2025 if her partner ran for the presidency. Salamé, who presents the news and was initially due to return on Monday, is expected to be replaced by Jean-Baptiste Marteau, the stand-in who has been in the chair this summer.

She has nonetheless insisted that she remains objective. "I am an independent and honest journalist, a free woman," she said in February, while acknowledging that questions about their personal and professional situation were "legitimate".

World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Extreme weather hits Europe as wildfires, floods and storms force thousands to evacuate
World.content:
Europe continues to struggle with the consequences of extreme weather, with Serbia, Bosnia, Spain, and Poland all facing severe conditions.

 

In Serbia, the EU has sent helicopters and firefighters to support local crews battling a blaze that has engulfed more than 1,600 hectares of vegetation in the Deliblatska Pescara nature reserve, 60 kilometres east of Belgrade. The effort is also being assisted by a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 water bomber deployed since Thursday, alongside several Serbian army helicopters.

"The situation is extremely difficult," says Ivica Dacic, Serbia's Interior Minister, adding that "more than 400 people are deployed there on a daily basis."

The crisis extends further into the region, where a large fire broke out on Saturday in the border area between Bosnia and Croatia. Bosnian police closed the main highway connecting Trebinje in Bosnia to Dubrovnik in Croatia, forcing thousands of tourists to turn back and alter their holiday plans.

Several villages around the small town of Ivanica were evacuated as the flames approached homes, and local firefighters reported that some livestock was caught in the fire and burnt. Croatian firefighters from nearby Dubrovnik arrived to assist Bosnian crews in battling the forest fire, which is spreading over an area more than 16 kilometres in diameter across narrow, difficult-to-access terrain. Supported by helicopters, emergency teams continue to fight the blaze, but relentless heat and strong winds have pushed the fire further inland. The Trebinje area has not seen rain for months, leaving the parched landscape exceptionally vulnerable during one of the hottest and driest summers in recent history.

Wildfires and floods in Spain

Meanwhile, Spain has faced a weekend of contrasting weather extremes. Torrential rain and flooding in Tarragona left 11 people injured and disrupted road and rail services after more than 145 mm fell in some areas. Further strong thunderstorms are forecast across eastern and northeastern Spain, while an unusually powerful Atlantic low is bringing heavy rain to Galicia.

Elsewhere in the country, firefighters in Spain’s eastern Valencia region continued battling intense wildfires. A blaze broke out in the town of Segorbe late Thursday after a lightning strike and began spreading rapidly Friday afternoon as winds shifted, leading authorities to raise the wildfire emergency to Level 2.

Personnel from Spain’s Military Emergency Unit and local fire departments joined the response, while more than 1,000 residents from the nearby town of Gatova were forced to evacuate over fears for their homes. Supported by aerial resources, crews have since managed to stabilise the fire after it burned around 630 hectares. The events mark a sharp shift from extreme heat earlier in the week, when temperatures reached up to 44°C.

Poland struggled, but the situation is improving

Further north, severe weather has also struck Poland. Since Friday, storms have wreaked havoc across the country, with firefighters responding to more than 6,500 incidents.

The storms hit residents in many areas, forcing the precautionary evacuation of 12 scout camps amid floods and power cuts. Brigadier Karol Kroć from the State Fire Service told the Polish Press Agency that no injuries have been reported so far.

On Sunday, storms are still expected in northern Poland, as the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management has issued yellow weather warnings for two small regions, with a local forecast of heavy rainfall up to 30 litres per square metre and wind gusts of up to 70 kilometres per hour. Hail is also possible in some areas. Ho

However, the general weather in the country on Sunday has improved significantly. Therefore, the weather conditions across the rest of Poland are expected to be much calmer.

World.title: Chinese humanoid robot beats Bolt's 100-metre world record time
World.content:
Step aside, Usain Bolt, there's a new speed king in town - TienKung the robot.

 

The Chinese humanoid, manufactured by the Beijing Centre for Humanoid Robotics, ran the 100 metres in 9.39 seconds at the World Humanoid Robot Games on Saturday, beating the Jamaican great's 9.58 world record time - which he set at the Olympiastadion in Berlin in 2009.

"This is a hugely impressive feat," organisers of the Beijing robot games wrote in a post on X, noting that last year's winning time clocked in at 21.50 seconds.

"In 1 year alone the robots competing have become twice as fast. This highlights the pace of advancement both in the market, and specifically in Chinese robotics," they added.

The World Humanoid Robot Games, held in Beijing's "Ice Ribbon" stadium, is bringing together 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries as they compete across events including athletics, boxing, football, weightlifting, and gymnastics.

Video footage of the robots has been shared widely on social media over the last few days, particularly clips showing the humanoids slamming into large mats and slowly falling backwards at the end of races.

While the rather amusing clips have been entertaining viewers, organisers of the games say people should be impressed.

"It shows a pace of technological advancement that almost beggars belief," they said. "Only a year ago, at the last WHRG, robots were slow, ponderous machines that struggled to complete a track sprint. This year they are expected to obliterate world records. The pace that the Chinese robotics industry is advancing at, much like the robot in the video shows no sign of deceleration".

Robots play soccer during the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, Sunday, Aug. 23, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

China has been leaning in hard to the humanoid robot industry, and investors appear to be on board.

Morgan Stanley Research has estimated that the humanoid market is likely to reach $5 trillion by 2050, with more than a billion of the robots potentially in use by then.

According to a report published by the bank last year, China is expected to have around 302.3 million humanoid robots in use by 2050.

World.title: Indian Coast Guard launches search and rescue operation after cargo vessel sinks in Bay of Bengal
World.content:
The Indian Coast Guard has launched a search and rescue operation off the coast of eastern India after a cargo ship sank in the Bay of Bengal.

 

According to the Coast Guard, the MV Ocean Winner vessel issued a distress alert while southeast off the port of Paradip on Saturday before contact was lost.

Two of the 24-strong crew have been rescued from life rafts, while the Coast Guard has deployed three ships to carry out surface searches for the remaining crew members.

The crew consisted of 20 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals, and one Bangladeshi, the agency said.

The cause of the sinking is not yet clear.

Sarbananda Sonowal, India's Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, said the Panama-flagged vessel had been carrying iron ore from the port of Paradip to China when it sank.

"All agencies are coordinating closely and actively doing search and rescue efforts. 2 survivors have been successfully rescued and are being given medical care; their rank and identity are currently being verified," he wrote in a post on X.

"My prayers for the safety of the remaining crew," he added.

World.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan strengthen ties as Israel tensions rise
World.content:
Tensions between Turkey and Israel have intensified after an Israeli airstrike targeted a Syrian military airbase near the Turkish border. The strike came days after Turkey’s new military pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

Advertising

Ankara swiftly condemned Tuesday's Israeli airstrike on Syria’s Abu Duhur military airbase, 70 kilometres from its border, calling it illegal and a breach of Syrian sovereignty.

Ankara is a key ally of Syria's new authorities. Israel justified its actions, accusing Turkey of seeking to expand its military footprint in Syria, which it sees as a serious threat.

“Israel is uneasy about the Turkish presence in Syria, and Turkish ambitions to play a major role in Syria’s future are unsettling from an Israeli perspective,” explains Turkey expert Gallia Lindenstrauss of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

“There's concern that Turkey will establish its own bases in Syria,” she added.

Israeli-Turkish tensions have risen over Israel’s war in Gaza and Lebanon, and Ankara’s support of Hamas, evolving into a broader regional rivalry.

“In general, there's uneasiness [in Israel] about Turkey's assertiveness, both in Syria and in the Mediterranean and other parts of the Middle East and the greater regional arena," said Lindenstrauss.

Landmark agreement

Earlier this month, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan made headlines by signing a landmark military accord in the Saudi city of Mecca. Known as the Mecca Accord, this alliance pledges mutual defence if any member is attacked, akin to NATO’s Article 5.

Turkish international relations expert Soli Ozel claims the impetus for the agreement is uncertainty around Washington’s willingness or ability to protect its regional allies amid ongoing tensions involving Iran.

“Undoubtedly, the United States is proving to be an increasingly unreliable partner. Countries worldwide, especially in the larger Middle East region, are looking for other ways to provide security for themselves,” said Ozel.

Iran says ‘Muslim Nato’ pact reflects retreat from US security umbrella

The Mecca Accord members view each other as bringing complementary strengths to deal with shared concerns.

"Pakistan brings military capabilities and is a nuclear power. The Saudis have the money. Turkey has a budding defence industry and a large army. It claims not to be against any country, but I think those three parties agree that Iran is a destabilising actor, as is Israel,” explained Ozel.

The Mecca Accord is set to boost defence and intelligence ties, with Saudi Arabia expected to bolster Turkey’s expanding defence sector.

But many analysts see Iran and Israel as the accord’s principal focus.

“The deal is meant to signal both to Iran and Israel that they will be isolated in the region if they continue with assertive, belligerent policies,” said Asli Aydintasbas of the United States-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey steps up as Europe's indispensable and uncomfortable defence partner

'Two axes in the Middle East'

Despite Iran’s recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aydintasbas argues that while the Mecca Accord has a mutual defence clause – meaning an attack on one member is an attack on all – Turkey and Pakistan will not be drawn into a conflict with Iran.

“We know that they have no desire to get involved. But it does mean there will be greater military cooperation,” said Aydintasbas.

Countering Houthi rebel attacks in the Red Sea on Saudi tankers could be the first real test of the alliance.

But Aydintasbas cautions that the Mecca Accord will not replace the US as the “ultimate security provider” for the region. Instead, it's more about burden sharing, a move that fits well with Washington’s wider agenda.

Washington has given its blessing to the accord, and expansion talks are already under way.

European Union slams 'inflammatory' Houthi Red Sea tanker attack

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hinted that Egypt could be the next member, with Turkish media reporting that Egypt’s foreign minister will join his Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani counterparts for a meeting in Istanbul later this month.

“Developments in Egypt are of major concern to Israel,” said Lindenstrauss. But she believes the Mecca Accord is an opportunity for Israel, given there are mutual concerns among its allies over the Accord.

“Israel already has very close relations with Greece, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates and India,” she noted. "And I do envision a deepening of this relationship. And so we have the formation of two loose axes in the Greater Middle East."

World.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy rejects wartime elections
World.content:
The Ukrainian president says wartime elections, as called for by the ex-defense minister, could "split Ukraine." He also said Russia was planning to mobilize hundreds of thousands of troops after September polls there.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that holding elections in his country amid the full-scale Russian invasion would be highly dangerous, in remarks made in response to a call from the former defense minister to organize a vote.

"I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in remarks released on Sunday.

Under martial law, elections are currently suspended in the country as it fights the invading Russian forces. The measure has wide public support.

What did Zelenskyy say about the proposed election?

"If we want to destroy the country, then we can move in the direction of elections during these times of war," Zelenskyy said in the firm rejection of the proposal by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

Fedorov made the call a month after being fired by Zelenskyy as defense minister.

Fedorov enjoys significant support among younger Ukrainians, thousands of whom have been calling for his reinstatement, with some saying he could seek to challenge Zelenskyy if an election did take place.

However, a recent poll showed that Zelenskyy would still be more popular as a presidential candidate.

Zelenskyy was critical of Fedorov in his remarks, saying: "I believe he is going himself — or is being pushed — toward wrong things."

Ukraine protests erupt over ouster of defense minister To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia planning mass mobilization — Zelenskyy

Zelenskyy also said that Kyiv believed Russia was planning to mobilize 300,000 more troops for its invasion after parliamentary elections take place in September.

He added that Moscow might draft hundreds of thousands more in 2027 as it seeks to capture the rest of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, one of its main strategic goals.

Unwilling soldiers: A stealth mass draft starting in Russia? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Agreement on missile interceptors from Germany

As Ukraine continues to come under intense missile attacks from its neighbor, Zelenskyy also spoke of having struck an agreement with Germany on the supply of 600 Patriot PAC-2 missile interceptors for 2027-28.

The announcement comes after German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visited Ukraine on Saturday.

The US Patriots are the only weapon in Kyiv's arsenal that can take on Russia's Iskander-M and Kinzhal ballistic missiles, but ammunition for the system is running short.

France on Saturday also promised to deliver new interceptor missiles.

As Europe seeks to fill the gap left by a US that, under Donald Trump, has shown ever more reluctance to help Ukraine, Norway has also said it plans to ‌give ⁠another ⁠85 billion Norwegian ​crowns ($9.2 billion; €7.8 billion) in ​financial ​support ‌to Kyiv in the 2027 ‌fiscal year.

World.title: Is the US seeing a turning point in obesity rates?
World.content:
Obesity rates climbed in the US for years, but now there are signs this could be changing. Use of weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy has increased rapidly — are they helping?

The United States has been grappling with an obesity epidemic since the late 1970s, but there is growing evidence that the constantly climbing obesity rates are beginning to drop.

"We're seeing signs that there's going to be a turning point," said Benjamin Rader, an epidemiologist at Boston Children's Hospital and at Harvard Medical School who conducts research into health trends using large datasets. In 2024, he and his colleagues published a study based on data from more than 16 million adults, which suggested there had been a decline in obesity prevalence in 2023 — for the first time in more than 10 years.

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey also indicated a slight decline between 2021 and 2023. More recent surveys have also provided evidence of declining figures.

Use of Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound skyrockets

This comes as a series of new drugs, which some people are using for weight loss, have come onto the market. The use of the GLP-1 agonist drugs Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound has increased rapidly in recent years in the US, with prescriptions more than quadrupling between 2021 and early 2026.

Some of the active ingredients in these drugs were originally developed to treat Type 2 diabetes by mimicking a naturally occurring intestinal hormone to promote a feeling of fullness and to slow down gastric emptying. This has led to many patients losing a significant amount of weight.

Weight-loss drugs Wegovy, Ozempic, Mounjaro boom in UK To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Rader, "it seemed like it [the impact of this medicine] was bound to show up in the data" and that it was possible to be "moderately confident that drugs themselves were having an effect."

'Strong evidence showing significant decline in obesity'

For Peminda Cabandugama, an endocrinologist and spokesperson for The Obesity Society, which provides support to professionals in the obesity field, "there is strong evidence showing that there is a significant decline in obesity."

In a written statement to DW, he said the "general opinion is that GLP-1 medications and their combinations and their increased use as well as the recent attention put on the importance of weight management have played a large and direct role in this reduction in obesity prevalence."

But for Rader there is no definitive proof of a causal relationship. He has no doubt that the drugs have led to weight loss in many people at an individual level, but he told DW that it was too soon to say whether it "will lead to a plateau, […] a decrease […] or a slower decrease in the next 20 years" and what the effect on the general population might be.

Cabandugama thinks the current figures might also have been influenced by lifestyle changes during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and points out that "these trends are likely a confluence of multiple elements that include the increased use of anti-obesity medications, post-pandemic behavioral changes, increased awareness about the importance of weight management etc."

Is the decline temporary?

Some researchers in the US don't believe obesity rates will decline permanently. A study by the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington in Seattle predicts a rise in rates through 2035 and suggests that the proportion of obese adults could increase from 42.5% in 2022 to 46.9% in 2035.

Though Rader doesn't necessarily consider such predictions to be wrong, he pointed out that many prediction models are based on data from before the boom in GLP-1 drugs and might not take into account their potential effects. In an article for the Journal of the American Medical Association, he warned that the models could overestimate the future burden of obesity.

The authors of the IHME study have not entirely dismissed this criticism, but they did point out that to date only a small proportion of obese people use such drugs and that many patients discontinue treatment within a year. They added that some people gain weight again after initially losing it, and more representative data was needed to assess whether such drugs will have a lasting effect on obesity rates.

Billions made from weight-loss injections To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Cabandugama has also urged caution, saying that while there are currently strong signs of a decline, "the general consensus is that it is still too early to tell whether this is a true trend reversal."

Consequences of decline in obesity rates would be far-reaching

Though for a long time, obesity was viewed primarily as a result of an individual's lifestyle, it has since become well-known that this complex chronic condition is caused by a combination of biological, genetic, social and psychological factors.

If the US were at a turning point, the consequences would be far-reaching. Weight loss in obese people does not only reduce their risk of related health problems, but also contributes to greater mobility, more independence and a higher quality of life.

For Cabandugama, "the health outcomes to improve first would be betterments in cardiometabolic parameters: blood glucose levels (Type 2 diabetes mellitus), cardiovascular outcomes, fatty liver, obstructive sleep apnea etc.," which in the long term could also reduce pressure on the healthcare system.

Regardless of whether rates are on the decline, Rader said "obesity still remains a huge public health crisis in America that deserves attention, deserves funding, and deserves alternative solutions, especially as we think about how GLP-1s are not accessible to all Americans based on price and other factors."

"A turning point does not mean that we're suddenly in the clear and that we don't have to worry about this thing anymore," he said.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?
World.content:
Germany's centrist parties reject any cooperation with the Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are classified as right-wing extremist. However, this policy is coming under increasing pressure.

A firewall is a wall designed to prevent a fire from spreading from one building to another. In German politics, the term "firewall" serves as a metaphor for a strict boundary drawn against parties regarded as extremist. Just as a firewall is intended to protect buildings from fire, the "political firewall" is intended to safeguard democracy.

Whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is in fact a party that is hostile to democracy has not yet been determined by the courts. While Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, has classified individual AfD state associations as "confirmed right-wing extremist," the question of whether the party as a whole is acting against the German constitution would have to be decided by the Federal Constitutional Court in proceedings to ban the party.

Calls for an AfD ban have been made repeatedly, but no formal application has been filed to date.

How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chancellor Merz is growing tired of the term 'firewall'

The term "political firewall" cannot be clearly attributed to any single originator. However, its widespread use is due in large part to Friedrich Merz.

Upon becoming leader of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in December 2021, for example, he told the German news magazine Der Spiegel: "Under my leadership, there will be a firewall against the AfD."

In 2018, the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility" at its party conference, rejecting "coalitions and similar forms of cooperation" with both the AfD and the socialist Left Party.

This did not apply only to formal agreements and coalitions with the AfD. At times, the CDU also deliberately sought majorities without AfD support, and CDU officeholders declined to be elected to political positions with AfD votes.

January 2025 marked a break from that path: A CDU motion in the Bundestag calling for the rejection of asylum seekers passed with AfD support. At the time, Merz was leader of the CDU and thus of the parliamentary opposition. To this day, critics continue to accuse him of breaching the firewall policy.

Now chancellor, Merz tends to avoid the term and has grown increasingly irritated by questions about it.

The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the ecologist Greens reject any cooperation with the AfD, although without formal resolutions to that effect. Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the left-wing populist Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW), takes a different stance. She explicitly opposes excluding the AfD and would even be willing to pave the way for an AfD-led government in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where elections will be held on September 6.





How Germany's Left Party is split over anti-Zionism To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

No firewall at the municipal level

The reliance on AfD votes by Merz's CDU in January 2025 triggered shock and outrage, but it wasn't the first time a politician who officially supports the firewall doesn't adhere to it in practice. In 2020, Thomas Kemmerich from the neoliberal FDP was elected Premier of Thuringia with AfD votes.

Angela Merkel, who was chancellor at the time, was alarmed and demanded that the election "must be reversed."

Kemmerich resigned just a few days later.

At the local level, however, the firewall is often highly permeable. In city and municipal councils, politicians from other parties have repeatedly voted alongside the AfD. Proponents of this more relaxed attitude often argue that, for example, building a daycare center does not become a bad idea simply because the AfD also supports it.

Critics, however, regularly warn of a gradual process of normalization. In their view, such cooperation makes the AfD socially acceptable, and what begins in local politics could eventually spread to state or even federal politics.

Can 40% of voters be ignored?

The firewall policy does not appear to be harming the AfD. On the contrary, its poll ratings continue to rise, despite, or perhaps even because of, the firewall.

When the AfD is particularly strong, as it is across much of eastern Germany, the other parties represented in state parliaments often have to join forces to prevent an AfD-led state government. This can come at the expense of the credibility of parties whose ideological positions are far apart.

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Political scientists also point to a democratic deficit if the political preferences of AfD voters are ignored over the long term.

Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) recently said of Saxony-Anhalt: "It is simply completely undemocratic to permanently exclude a party supported by around 40% of voters. The firewall has failed."

Some CDU politicians in eastern Germany have questioned the rationale behind the firewall. The Brandenburg branch of the Small and Medium Enterprises and Economic Union, an internal CDU interest group, recently submitted a motion calling on the party "at the federal level to work toward repealing or fundamentally revising the CDU's incompatibility resolution vis-a-vis the AfD."

Following strong criticism from the federal party leadership, the group withdrew the motion.

Saxony's CDU Premier Michael Kretschmer, who leads a minority government in Dresden, recently told the German business daily Handelsblatt: "Anyone still talking about firewalls has failed to recognize the signs of the times. We need to talk to everyone who is willing to talk."

At the federal level, the CDU would prefer to put an end to such debates altogether. Thorsten Frei, the new chair of the Bundestag's conservative parliamentary group, which includes the Christian Social Union (CSU), has made clear that he will not tolerate deviations by individual state branches.

"The ban on cooperation with the AfD is a fundamental party resolution of the CDU. It cannot be interpreted differently from one federal state to another," he told newspapers belonging to the Funke Media Group.

The chancellor, too, is holding firm now. Despite the immense pressure and the challenging political landscape in eastern Germany, and aside from the break in January 2025, he continues to uphold the resolution of incompatibility with both the AfD and the Left Party.

How governing majorities opposed to the AfD can be formed in the future therefore remains an open question.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Kazakhstan parliamentary vote to cement president's power
World.content:
Candidates from seven state-approved parties are taking part in the election, while opposition parties have been banned. Central Asia's largest nation, Kazakhstan maintains a delicate balance between Russia and the West.

Kazakhstan's 12.3 million eligible voters will elect the Central Asian country's parliament on Sunday.

The polls come after a new constitution approved in March did away with the Senate to create a new unicameral Kurultai — a reference to the medieval councils of the region's nomadic past.

Backers of the new body say it will give parliament more say in decision making, critics argue it will only cement the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

The 73-year-old took the reins from authoritarian Nursultan Nazarbayev — who himself ruled the country for 30 years after the collapse of the Soviet Union — in 2019.

The constitutional reform also opens the door for President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to stay in power Image: Turar Kazangapov/REUTERS

The pro-presidential Adilet party is expected to win an overwhelming majority in Sunday's vote, with a number of smaller parties loyal to Tokayev also pegged to enter parliament.

Seven state-approved parties have been allowed to field candidates for the 145-seat parliament while genuine opposition parties have been banned.

The election is taking place amid soaring inflation (which is hovering around 10.2%) and rising taxes, fueling concerns for the government — and particularly Tokayev — of a repeat of January 2022 cost of living unrest that left 238 protesters and police dead.

Inequality, corruption led to Kazakhstan unrest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Press crackdown and financial strain color Kazakhstan's election

Beyond financial strain, Sunday's vote is also taking place against the background of crackdowns on press freedom, with numerous reporters under house arrest and official criminal cases being brought against 10 independent journalists and bloggers.

Tokayev, a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who worked at the UN, has touted his reforms and justified the many changes he has initiated — including the introduction of the new constitution — as necessary in a fast-changing world.

"Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in our country's history," said Tokayev on Friday.

"Amid unprecedented geopolitical tensions and mounting global challenges, we must firmly and consistently implement our strategy to transform Kazakhstan into a truly developed state," he added.

Tokayev has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow — with their shared Soviet ties — and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Resource-rich and strategically located Kazakhstan also has ties to China and the European Union.

Although Tokayev has said that he has no plans of staying in power beyond his current term, the constitutional reform that 87% of voters backed this March effectively reset term limits for the office — making him eligible to run for another seven-year stint in 2029 should he change his mind.

World.title: Search resumes for 22 crew after cargo ship sinks off India
World.content:
The Panama‑flagged Ocean Winner had 24 people on board when it sank in the Bay of Bengal. The ship is thought to have been carrying iron ore from India to Singapore.

A search-and-rescue operation was continuing on Sunday after a cargo ship sank off the eastern coast of India.

The Panama-flagged vessel Ocean Winner had 24 crew on board when it sank on Friday. Two Chinese nationals were rescued on Saturday, with 22 people still unaccounted for, the Indian Coast Guard said.

The two rescued Chinese seafarers said the vessel developed a list on Friday and ​sank within eight minutes, forcing crew to abandon ship, said Shyam Jagannathan, ​director general of India's Maritime Administration.

'Developing a list' is a technical maritime term which means the vessel began tilting. The cause for this was not immediately known.

Search on for missing crew members

The chances of finding survivors fell sharply after 12 hours, but rescuers were continuing the search, Jagannathan ​said.

The missing crew members include 18 ‌Chinese ​nationals, three Myanmar nationals

and one Bangladeshi, according to the Indian Coast Guard. In a post on X, it said it had deployed three ships to conduct surface searches for the remaining crew members.

According to officials cited in the Indian Express, the ship was about 240 nautical miles (444 kilometers, 276 miles) off the coast of Odisha.

According to ship-tracking app MarineTraffic, the Ocean Winner was carrying iron ore from Paradip port in Odisha to Singapore.

World.title: Trump hits out at Canada over retaliatory tariffs
World.content:
Donald Trump has accused Canada of treating US farmers unfairly for years as a trade standoff between Ottawa and Washington escalates. Both sides are threatening new tariffs after the collapse of talks on Friday.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday accused Canada of wanting "the benefits of being a [US] State, without being one" in his first remarks since trade talks between Ottawa and Washington failed.

"They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!" he wrote on his social media platform Truth Social.

What has happened in the US-Canada trade dispute?

In an ongoing trade dispute with the United States, Canada said on Saturday that it would introduce tariffs on several US products starting September 8.

The announcement comes in retaliation to the US imposing 50% tariffs earlier on Saturday on a broad range of Canadian products after the two sides failed to reach a trade deal on Friday.

"Canada will match Washington's new ⁠tariffs ​dollar for dollar in order to protect ​Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Ottawa.

"In the coming days, we will release the details of these new tariff measures, which will come into force the Tuesday after Labor Day," he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the proposed trade deal was 'uneconomic, unfair and undermined the net benefits for Canada' Image: Chris Tanouye/REUTERS

While the US had blamed Canada for declining to finalize the trade pact with Washington on Friday, Carney defended Ottawa's position, explaining, "We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked."

He later on Saturday met virtually with provincial and territorial premiers to discuss the suspension of the trade talks with the US.

What products are affected by the tariffs?

The US tariffs will affect a broad range of products, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing ‌rods, and hockey ​equipment, and cover some $20 billion (€17 billion) worth of Canadian exports to its southern neighbor.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs would, in turn, target steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, Carney said.

The US currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports, making Ottawa potentially more vulnerable in the standoff Carney explicitly described as a trade "war."

"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.

How have Canadian and US politicians reacted?

Doug Ford, the premier of Canada's most populous province Ontario and one of the most vocal opponents of US President Donald Trump's tariffs, slammed the proposed trade deal and backed Carney's decision to retaliate.

"I'm glad he didn't sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector and ​manufacturing sector," Ford said on Saturday.

Meanwhile, Pierre Poilievre, the leader of the official opposition Conservative Party, urged Canadians to "stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses."

In the US, Democratic lawmakers and governors have blamed Trump for the escalating trade conflict.

"Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That's Trump's economic policy in a nutshell," New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted on X.

Michigan Congresswoman Haley Stevens also slammed "Trump's reckless and unnecessary trade war."

Friendly ties turned sour

The fresh tariffs are the culmination of long and tense trade negotiations between the two sides and mark a sharp reversal from just two days earlier, when officials from Washington and Ottawa appeared optimistic that a compromise was in the making.

According to the AP news agency, no further talks were planned to resolve the situation.

The US administration's approach to Canada is a major change from the friendly ties the two countries have traditionally had.

During a 2025 Washington trip, Carney was still all smiles — but tensions appear to have worsened Image: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

Trump has often said he wants tariffs on Canadian goods to encourage companies to move manufacturing back to the US.

He has also made controversial comments about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney said Canada understood that "America has changed" and that the two countries would "not return to their old relationship."

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Wesley Dockery

World.title: Australia confirms H5N1 bird flu case in local mammal
World.content:
Australian authorities said the deadly virus's spread to mammals was "concerning" but "not unexpected."

Australia confirmed its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a mammal on Sunday, after it found the deadly virus in a long-nosed fur seal.

Authorities in the state of South Australia said they found the virus in the seal in the coastal town of Beachport, about 310 kilometers (192 miles) from the state capital, Adelaide.

Austrialia has been combating the highly pathogenic influenza after it arrived in the country in June. Earlier this month it reported its first mass seabird deaths, marking an escalation.

What did authorities have to say?

There are an estimated 100,000 long-nosed fur seals in the state's waters. The infected individual was found dead with no signs of injury, authorities said.

Its death "does not ‌appear to be associated with other sick or dead ‌marine mammals," Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said in televised remarks.

"Once the H5 bird flu is spreading in the natural environment it is not possible to avoid significant losses," Collins added.

"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected for us to start to see infection in other wildlife, particularly in marine mammals, particularly in areas where there are high infection rates in wild birds," Collins was quoted by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation as saying.

Australia began vaccinating its birds against the deadly virus earlier this month Image: Phillip Island Nature Parks/AFP

The virus has not spread to Australia's poultry or agriculture, according to the government, which counted 297 confirmed cases as of Friday.

Earlier in August, the government said it would begin a bird vaccination program based on the species' vulnerability to the virus and conservation impact.

World.title: Red faces as Sydney Marathon medal shows German stadium
World.content:
A medal minted for finishers in the Sydney Marathon features a skyline of the city — with one landmark from rather far away. Organizers say the muddle only makes the medal "a little more unique."

Organizers of the 2026 Sydney Marathon are making the best of the situation after minting tens of thousands of medals engraved with depictions of landmarks from the eastern Australian city along with one that doesn't belong — the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany.

The medal should have instead shown the Allianz Stadium in Sydney, which is one of the sights that participants in the upcoming race will pass while running the the 42.2-kilometer (26.2-mile) course.

More than 40,000 participants are expected to earn the medal as a "badge of honor" for completing the race on August 30.

Other landmarks shown include the famous Opera House and the Sydney Harbour Bridge.

Sydney's Allianz Stadium also has its own unique appearance Image: Rafael Ben Ari/Newscom/picture alliance

What have organizers said about the medal mix-up?

"A little too much international flavor has found its way onto the back of the finishers medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium," a Sydney Marathon spokesperson said.

"We're not going to run from it, it was an unfortunate error; though it's certainly given everyone somehing to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humor," the spokesperson said.

"With the event a week away, this is the medal our finishers will receive."

"Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget," the spokesperson added.

"It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."

Good-humored reaction from Munich

Munich's Allianz Arena has responded in light-hearted manner.

"Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!" it posted on Instagram.

"Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena — Sydney Opera — Unique Architecture — Both are worth a visit!"

The daily Sydney Morning Herald also came up with a gleefully teasing headline: "The medal that will put Sydney on the map. The wrong map."

The other side of the medal shows shows a gold-and-indigo pattern by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian that has been widely commended.

Killian has said he was not involved in the design of the side showing the landmarks.
