World.title: Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018905/Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.content:
Poorly animated yellow cows walking on two legs, raw voice acting, and extremely slow pace — these are characteristics of China’s most recent box office hit and viral phenomenon.

Released Aug. 5 after virtually no promotion, the movie, “Niu Lai,” or “Cow Comes,” is named for its titular character: a calf who struggles to stand. The film follows Niu Lai and his herd as they overcome a number of difficulties while migrating, eventually growing up into an able-bodied adult cow unfazed in the face of danger. Except, Niu Lai awakens, realizing that he is still a calf — but he is finally able to support his own weight.

The movie, reported to have no financial backing, earned just 5,500 yuan ($815) at the box office in its first week. But after multiple viewers posted images of the film on social media criticizing it, that number suddenly surged to over 710,000 yuan on Aug. 15, according to ticketing platform Maoyan. As of Tuesday afternoon, it has taken in 20 million yuan, a figure projected to grow to 135 million yuan by the time it leaves screens.

The reason for its explosive popularity? Its absurdist visuals and overall crude production design have turned it into a word-of-mouth viral phenomenon. The characters’ legs rarely move in sync, making them appear like they’re sliding. Close-ups of their heads are overblown and blurry. Transitions between scenes are jarring and illogical, and the characters’ voices are poorly recorded and overly stilted.

The effect has led to highly polarized ratings on domestic review platform Douban, with many giving it either one or five stars. As one highly upvoted comment on Maoyan reads, “You don’t have to watch bad movies, but when a movie is bad enough, you have to.”

Wang Yunfei, the founder of a cartoon studio and an acting animated film judge at various film festivals, told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper, “Professional animators couldn’t produce something this poorly even if they made mistakes. So from a professional standpoint, there’s really nothing to critique. It’s just spectacle-watching.”

The movie’s unexpectedly raw, homemade production has also been regarded by critics and viewers alike as a rebuke to high-investment but poorly reviewed films.

“Niu Lai” was produced by Jingyuan Culture Film and Television Media, based in the northeastern city of Dalian, which was converted from a one-person renovation company, according to corporate data platform Qichacha.

The renovator in question is the film’s creator, 34-year-old Xin Yumeng, who made it alongside his mother, Sun Lifang. The pair reportedly had no background in animation and made the film over five years, without the help of AI. They also provided the voices for the characters, while Sun composed and sang the film’s theme song.

On a domestic radio show, Xin said that he made the film out of a love for animated films, and chose a cow as the protagonist because his father was born in the Year of the Ox.

As for the quality of the film, Xin added that much of the equipment he bought secondhand for the film’s production eventually broke down. “Even the computer motherboards burned out ... The final result has a lot to do with the equipment used.”

Le Fumin, a 35-year-old security worker from Shanghai, told domestic media that he liked that “Niu Lai” was made by two ordinary people, rather than having large film-industry backing. “It shows a bit of rebellion against the assembly-line formula of mainstream filmmaking,” he said. “Why should I only be allowed to watch what the industry feeds me? The kind of happiness I choose for myself is worth the ticket price, too.”

Le said the atmosphere in the theater was particularly relaxed. “Over the course of two hours, the pressure of meeting KPIs at work, the exhaustion of commuting, and all the troubles of everyday life just melted away with the laughter of the whole theater,” he said. “It felt like returning to something simple and genuine — like the carefree feeling of watching random films in a video rental shop as a kid.”

As “Niu Lai” has risen in popularity, fan-made tributes to it have spread online and offline, with some placing Niu Lai into posters for recent international box office hits such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey.” Cinema staff have also put up rudimentary, hand-drawn posters advertising the film — and paying homage to its crude animation — outside theaters.

Even stocks of three companies with “niu” in their names — Jinniu Chemical Industry, Goneo Group, and Tongniu Information — shot into the top five trending list on domestic finance data platform Tonghuashun over the weekend, as the film’s title can be interpreted as “the bull market is coming,” domestic media reported.

Other entities are also capitalizing on the film’s virality, creating their own animal-based animated shorts to promote products. On Monday, local authorities for Dongguan City in the southern Guangdong province produced a video titled “E Lai,” or “Goose Comes,” to promote the city’s local specialty — roast goose — garnering more than 26,000 likes on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok.

For most, however, the movie is simply about having fun. Mak SzeNing, a 27-year-old pet care worker from Hong Kong, watched the film in the eastern city of Hangzhou at a nearly sold-out screening. “I don’t think the movie’s value lies in its production quality,” she told Sixth Tone. “Its value is that it brings a group of strangers into the same theater, and suddenly everyone feels like they’ve found their kindred spirits and laughs together.”

“If a movie can make people laugh, then I think it’s a good movie,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “Niu Lai.” From Douban)

World.title: For poet-singer Toni Panagu, art begins as ideas you gamble on
World.content:
Panagu often finds himself contending with a blank page to write his next poem or next song, and it's his sheer curiosity that allows him to keep things moving

Multi-disciplinary creative Toni Panagu approaches art with a trusty guitar and a way with words that translates beautifully in rhythm and rhyme.

Poetry had been in Panagu’s life for as long as he could remember. In school, whenever the lectures were starting to get boring, he would busy himself with writing poems at the back of his notebook instead of drifting off to sleep. For a time, these lines would never really escape these bound sheets of paper, until a friend suggested that he start posting them on Facebook.

Eventually, he would join an organization, Linangan sa Imahen, Retorik, at Anyo (LIRA), where he would learn the conventions of traditional poetry. Soon after, he would start pursuing his craft on his own terms, and before long, would start writing his own lyrics, too.

“’Yung tatay ko, binilhan ako ng murang gitara sa Surplus (My father bought me a cheap guitar from Surplus),” he said as he pointed out his father seated a few rows away from us in the auditorium where he had just finished performing.

With his own guitar and a pirated CD of The Beatles’ greatest hits, Panagu would then teach himself how to play these songs strum by strum, and chord by chord.

“[May] gitara tapos ang dami kong mga words. Pinagsama ko na. Ginawa ko nang kanta ‘yung tula,” he shared.

(I had a guitar and a lot of words to say. I just put them together. I turned my poems into songs.)

While all this was happening, though, Panagu shared he didn’t know how to sing yet. “I’m serious!” he said in Filipino when I told him I found that hard to believe.

Panagu would cringe at the sound of his own voice before he finally found the confidence to start releasing his original music in 2022. But he attests that the cringe was absolutely necessary for him to test the bounds of his vocals — and define his own sonic profile as we know it today.

But it’s Panagu’s range as a songwriter that’s most fascinating. The one thing that drives it all? Curiosity.

Curiosity fuels the artist

Inspiration is everywhere if you just know how to look. For Panagu, much of it comes from other mediums of art — in the films he watches, the music he listens to, and the paintings he comes across. He is a firm believer in the literary concept of ekphrasis, where an artist is compelled to produce their own art in response to an already existing piece of art. He had once even written a poem inspired by Clairo’s song “Juna” from her 2024 record Charm.

But it’s the human condition that often shapes the music Panagu makes. He has a whole catalogue of love songs on Spotify, but also has several political anthems under his belt.

“Ideas come to me as often as I wake up,” Panagu said when asked how his best ideas come to him. “Hindi naman lahat ng idea nagiging art pero araw-araw may naiisip tayo. So kailangan lang natin isugal ‘yung idea na ‘yun para maging art siya.”

(Not all ideas become art but we think of things every day. We just need to gamble on that idea to turn it into art.)

What may be Panagu’s most noteworthy piece of work yet, however, is the song he performed at the 2026 FILSCAP Songwriters’ Night Select.

When it came time for the poet-singer to finally do his big number, he had almost immediately strode around from one part of the stage to the next as he sang a fast-paced track about attachment issues and the ills of modern dating. It’s upbeat, and its lyrics come to you faster than you can realize that he’s basically trying to say that sometimes, you’re not actually in love. You’re just attached.

Play Video

The song is entitled “Breadcrumbs,” and it plays around with the buzzwords “love bomb” and “trauma dump” to get the point across. Panagu had finished his big number by fake collapsing on the wooden stage as the lights dimmed — earning loud cheers and several standing ovations from the audience.

Yet the process for creating “Breadcrumbs” wasn’t as glamorous as you might think. We often picture the conception of art as this sacred ritual where the singer has to shut themselves into a quiet room to harness the crucial details that will make up the whole song. While it may be true for some artists, things happened a little differently for Panagu.

“Akala natin na sobrang entertaining process ‘yung paggawa pero minsan boring lang siya na nakaupo ka, may gitara ka, tapos talagang kukutkutin mo lang. Bagay ba tong salita na ‘to? Bagay ba ‘tong chord na ‘to? Uupuan mo talaga siya. Minsan kapag hindi mo pa madugtungan, hayaan mo muna. Medyo ganun ‘yung nangyari sa akin sa ‘Breadcrumbs,’” Panagu shared.

(We think creation is such an entertaining process but sometimes it’s boring. You’re just seated, you have a guitar, and you’re there to pick the song apart. Does this word fit? Does this chord fit? You really have to sit on it. Sometimes when you can’t complete the song, you just have to let it be. That’s kind of what happened to me with “Breadcrumbs.”)

The initial puzzle pieces of “Breadcrumbs” emerged while Panagu was in line to pay off the next installment for his motorcycle. He was able to finish the first part of the chorus right then and there, but these waves of creativity can sometimes go as quickly as they come.

It had taken him another week to complete the first verse, and two weeks later, he had the second verse. A little bit later, he thought of adding the bridge, too. All it took was a little patience for everything to slowly come together — until it finally reached the FILSCAP stage.

Blank pages

Panagu is an artist through and through. Nobody is in tune with his own craft more than he is, and it allows him to create a distinction between the many forms of art he puts out into the world.

But they all start the same way. Whether you’re writing poetry or songs, it’s always the blank page you have to contend with first.

“Kapag nagsusulat ka, iba ‘yung approach mo sa language. Kasi ‘pag poetry, oo syempre, hahabulin mo ‘yung cadence, hahabulin mo ‘yung rhymes. Depende rin anong form ng poetry. Pero somehow ‘yung songs, may element siya ng pitch. So kailangan mong mag-assign ng mga nota doon sa mga salita. Ibang klaseng pag-iisip di siya.” he explained.

(When you write, you have a different approach to language. Because when it comes to poetry, of course, you’re after the cadence and rhymes. It depends on the form of poetry, too. But somehow, with songs, there’s an element of pitch. So you need to assign specific notes to specific words. It requires a different kind of thinking.)

Panagu’s almost relentless urge to keep creating has brought him to the right set of readers and the right set of listeners, and he couldn’t be happier.

Even then, he remains as grounded as ever. He’s made it clear that he doesn’t do what he does for public approval. Art requires a different kind of motivation to keep doing, and for Panagu, it’s life in general that sustains his craft.

For as long as he lives, then, Panagu will continue to create. – Rappler.com

World.title: Saudel may enter PAR as super typhoon on August 24
World.content:
FORECAST. PAGASA Weather Specialist Charmagne Varilla explains the bureau's 4 pm forecast for the three tropical cyclones outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility on August 23, 2026.

Typhoon Saudel is located 1,950 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon at 3 pm on Sunday, August 23, still outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility

MANILA, Philippines – The tropical cyclone with the international name Saudel could enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) as a super typhoon on Monday, August 24.

As of Sunday afternoon, August 23, Saudel remains a typhoon outside PAR. It was located 1,950 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon at 3 pm, moving northwest at a relatively fast 30 kilometers per hour (km/h).

So far, Saudel has maximum sustained winds of 165 km/h and gustiness of up to 205 km/h. But it could strengthen into a super typhoon before its possible entry into the northeastern corner of PAR, which may happen either Monday morning or afternoon.

Saudel is likely to remain far from Philippine landmass, and may already exit PAR on Tuesday, August 25. But PAGASA added that the tropical cyclone might stay inside PAR beyond Tuesday — just along the northern boundary — if its track shifts westward. It could also be downgraded back to a typhoon around this time.

Although Saudel is not expected to directly affect weather and sea conditions in the country, it is seen to eventually enhance the southwest monsoon or habagat, which has been weak since Thursday, August 20, but is still affecting Luzon.

Due to the southwest monsoon, PAGASA warned of moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters) in the country’s northernmost province of Batanes from Sunday afternoon to Monday afternoon.

On Sunday evening, the southwest monsoon is also bringing scattered rain and thunderstorms to the rest of Cagayan Valley, Metro Manila, the Ilocos Region, the Cordillera Administrative Region, Central Luzon, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro, as well as isolated rain showers or thunderstorms to the rest of Luzon.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Charmagne Varilla said the expected enhancement of the southwest monsoon may trigger significant rainfall starting Wednesday, August 26.

Meanwhile, Saudel’s local name would depend on the movement of another tropical cyclone — the tropical depression right outside the PAR eastern boundary.

This tropical depression was last spotted 1,265 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon at 3 pm on Sunday. It is currently moving east northeast or away from PAR at 15 km/h, but if it ends up heading toward PAR, it could enter before Saudel.

The next tropical cyclone that enters PAR would be given the local name Obet. After Obet, the next name on PAGASA’s list is Pilandok.

At the moment, the tropical depression has maximum sustained winds of 55 km/h and gustiness of up to 70 km/h.

There is also another tropical depression with the same maximum sustained winds and gustiness outside PAR — the former Neneng, which had weakened into a low pressure area last Thursday, then redeveloped into a tropical depression on Saturday, August 22.

Neneng, which was given the international name Gaenari, was located 520 kilometers north of Itbayat, Batanes, as of 3 pm on Sunday. It is moving southwest toward China at 25 km/h, and still has no impact on the Philippines.

Even when Neneng was inside PAR, it did not directly affect the country and only enhanced the southwest monsoon for a couple of days.

PAGASA previously estimated that up to four tropical cyclones may develop within or enter PAR in August. So far, there have been three during the month: Tropical Depression Luis, Tropical Storm Maymay (Kujira), and Neneng. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] The least we can do covering school shootings
World.content:
The least we can do as a newsroom is to cover responsibly, to the best of our judgment and abilities, and not add to the grief, especially of families who are experiencing the loss and of the affected communities

I write this newsletter sharing the mix of grief, terror, and trauma that every Filipino family and community must be going through right now. We see a surge of school violence across the country this year alone.

Freshest in our consciousness are the shootings at the Ateneo de Zamboanga and the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City. (But there are more: LIST: Cases of school violence in the Philippines in 2026)

All victims were students — young lives with so much promise. All the injured were students, once having a bright picture of the world but will now be carrying emotional wounds for a long time, maybe (hopefully not) even for the rest of their lives. All perpetrators were students — fellow learners with whom other students thought they’d be safe around.

The incidents happened in public and private schools, in cities separated by at least six provinces — walang pinipili (no place is safer than the other, so to speak).

The least we can do as a newsroom is to cover responsibly, to the best of our judgment and abilities, and not add to the grief, especially of families who are experiencing the loss and of the affected communities. We strive to do our part, through our reporting and engagement, in what psychological, social, and policy experts say is a whole range of systemic reforms we need to put in place before a child gets their hands on a gun and before the gun reaches the school gates.

READ:

You must be wondering how we’re navigating the coverage of sensitive incidents like these. And I will be honest with you, dear reader, that each situation presents us with a new nuance or complication that challenges what we thought we had figured how to handle in the last coverage.

The basics are there — thanks to various media watchdogs here and abroad that have crafted guidelines for covering incidents of school shootings, minors who are either victims or perpetrators of crime, and people harming themselves.

When the violence involves minors as attackers and victims, we do not name them, and do not cite personal details beyond what’s necessary and will not make them identifiable.

In the case of Zamboanga, we only cited the age and class levels of the students. We only carried the government position, not the name, of the shooter’s father to establish how he got hold of licensed guns. (It will be another judgement call if and when the father is called to a Senate hearing.) We set aside the intention to honor the victim, a bright and bemedalled student, with a profile to respect the family’s wishes for privacy, and for their security.

In the case of Tacloban, we stuck to just mentioning the ages of the shooters, and did not name them despite the identity of their aunt who owned the guns was revealed by the authorities and she was called to a Senate hearing. We were able to run short profiles of the victims because their families agreed to what we believe was their own way of processing their grief and honoring their children.

READ:

We refused to post the heartbreaking photos that could add to the families and the communities’ grief and could either traumatize or desensitize the broader audience. It was a hard no to the video of the attack being carried out. We’ve opened our opinion section to specialists who are looking at the issue from a lens that’s broader than just beefing up security in schools and the education department hiring more counselors (which are not bad, definitely).

Still, we sometimes trip, whether it be in a headline or video caption that miss contexts or nuances — and for that Rappler deeply apologizes.

As with our policy, we correct and apologize for them as soon as we realize the mistakes or our supportive audience calls our attention to them. We acknowledge the hurt and rage that offended communities express, even as we beat ourselves up for not having done better.

Please trust us, though, that in our core, we Rapplers and like-minded journalists are one with every community in doing the best we can to hopefully put an end to violence threatening our children, our schools, our environments.

If there is one area where I would admit we may have failed, then it’s in how, communicators that we are, we don’t have the perfect words to express how we grieve with you.

It is a time of dread, doubt, and distress. Please allow us to continue holding hands with you through all these. – Rappler.com

Inside the Newsroom is a newsletter delivered straight to your inbox every week. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to manage your newsletter subscriptions.

World.title: Canada to retaliate for US tariffs, worsening ties after talks fail
World.content:
US-CANADA. File photo shows President Donald Trump and Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, in October 2025.

'You're at war when you get attacked, we got attacked,' Prime Minister Mark Carney says when asked a question about whether Canada was engaged in a trade war

Canada will impose tariffs on some US goods in retaliation for 50% levies ordered by President Donald Trump on Canadian products, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Saturday, August 22, after trade talks collapsed between the two neighbors.

The “dollar for dollar” tariffs on imports of US steel, electronics and other products, to take effect on September 8, mark a further worsening of relations between the longtime allies and major trading partners.

The two countries failed to reach a trade deal late on Friday, August 21, with each side blaming the other for derailing three days of intensive negotiations. The breakdown complicates the future of a US-Mexico-Canada free-trade pact.

Trump’s new tariffs hit sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment, covering some $20 billion of Canadian exports to the US. These duties do not exempt Canadian products under the three-nation trade deal, which has shielded most Canadian exports to the US in the last 18 months.

‘We got attacked,’ Carney says

“Canada will match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses,” Carney told a press conference.

“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said when asked a question about whether Canada was engaged in a trade war.

Carney is one of the few global leaders to retaliate against US tariffs and has pledged to forge new trade and military alliances, despite Canada’s dependence on the United States for nearly 70% of its exports.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called the breakdown “a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States,” saying no new talks were planned with Canada.

“We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation,” Greer told Fox News. “They’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that.”

The White House, the US commerce secretary’s office and the US trade representative’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Canada will impose tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, along with some products the US previously targeted in Canada, Carney said from Ottawa’s Parliament building. The government will release details on its response in the coming days, he said.

“We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked,” Carney said.

Trump had expressed hope that a deal with Canada could happen on Friday.

But Carney said the US administration’s last-minute demands halted progress.

“In recent days, the US proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits to Canada, calling into question the reliability of any deal,” he said, adding these demands included curtailing Canada’s ability to forge new trade deals.

Larger vehicles, other sticking points

Carney said Canada would announce support measures next week for industries hit by the new US duties, adding these measures could last years.

The new US tariffs cover around 5% of Canada’s exports to the USThey could expose some vulnerable industries such as softwood lumber and wine to severe damage and lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts have said.

“We will be mobilizing our network of businesses in all regions and all sectors to brace for impact and make the best of a bad situation,” said Candace Laing, CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of the most vocal opponents of US tariffs, supported Carney’s decision to retaliate.

“I’m glad he didn’t sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector, and manufacturing sector,” Ford told reporters on Saturday.

One of the main sticking points was the treatment of larger vehicles.

Three sources said Canada wanted favorable tariff terms proposed for light-duty vehicles to extend to medium- and heavy-duty trucks, something the US resisted. Carney said the US position would have excluded Canadian-made models, including Ford’s F-350, F-450 and F-550 trucks and General Motors’ Silverado, making Canadian production less competitive.

There were also US proposals that affected Canadian culture, language and sovereignty, Carney said, without elaborating.

Carney was elected last year on a promise to be a tough negotiator with Trump, and remains broadly popular. Polls show most Canadians oppose making any concessions to the US.

“Canadians must stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses,” Pierre Poilievre, the leader of the official opposition Conservative Party, said in a statement. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kim Custodio turns from jiu-jitsu late bloomer to 4-time world champion
World.content:
What began as an effort to turn her ‘unhealthy’ lifestyle around has paved the way for Filipino jiu-jitsu standout Kimberly Anne Custodio to become a four-time world champion

Obsession may be the word Kimberly Anne Custodio would pick.

When it comes to jiu-jitsu, she lives and breathes the sport. She trains at least three times a day, and even on her supposed “rest days,” she trains twice. On top of that, she runs her own gym.

Her dedication is evident in the results.

In the 2026 Ju-Jitsu International Federation World Championships held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, this August, Custodio captured the gold medal in the adult female 45kg division for the third straight year and the fourth time overall.

All that despite being on the cusp of 40.

“My whole life revolves around jiu-jitsu. I do it every single day. When I don’t train, it feels like I’m losing my mind,” Custodio told Rappler in a mix of Filipino and English. “I genuinely enjoy it. I don’t think of it as tiring. After years of enjoying and training consistently, the results speak for themselves.”

Late bloomer

But the 39-year-old Custodio was not always the jiu-jitsu junkie.

Over a decade ago, Custodio worked in the marketing department of a prominent casino resort in Metro Manila and led what she described as an “unhealthy” lifestyle. Eventually, clothes could no longer fit, and even relatives couldn’t recognize her from afar.

But when a then 27-year-old Custodio got lightheaded from doing a simple task, she knew something has to change.

“When I tied my shoes and I started getting short of breath and my vision began to black out, that’s when it really clicked for me that I couldn’t keep living like this. I had to do something about it. I didn’t want to die young,” she said.

“I want to stay young forever.”

So Custodio set out to transforming her life and reshape her fitness as she pursued boxing and muay thai. She liked combat sports so much that she wanted to compete in mixed martial arts, but one of her coaches told her she needed to learn jiu-jitsu first.

Custodio and jiu-jitsu turned out to be a perfect match.

“I felt really unhealthy. Work was exhausting and toxic, and then you go home completely drained, only to wake up and do the same thing all over again the next day. You start to feel like a robot,” said Custodio.

“When I tried martial arts, especially jiu-jitsu, I felt like I had a goal every day. Especially when I became a national athlete, I felt that I wasn’t just competing for myself anymore — I was carrying the country. I was representing the entire nation.”

Jiu-jitsu is life

Custodio made the national team at 30 years old in 2018, then won her first world title at 35 years old in 2022 in UAE. She became so enamored with the sport that she left her day job to focus on being a national athlete.

“It feels really different when you’re representing the Philippines — you’re carrying the whole country with you. And that makes you want to keep getting better and better,” she said.

But as with any elite athlete, losses are inevitable as Custodio failed to defend her throne in the 2023 edition in Mongolia.

And yet, that particular defeat, or any loss for that matter, hardly discouraged her. If anything, Custodio embraces setbacks as opportunities to gauge where she stands and identify areas for improvement.

She never lost in the world championships since, ruling in 2024 in Greece, in 2025 in Thailand, and in 2026 in UAE as she racked up 10 consecutive victories.

“When I lose a competition, I don’t actually get sad. I get more excited instead and I think about how I lost and how to make my technique better,” said Custodio. “It’s like solving a puzzle. It’s not ideal when you keep winning because you start to wonder, ‘Am I really that good?’ When you lose, that’s when you grow. Whenever I lose, I’m sure that in my next competition, I’m unbeatable.”

At 39, Custodio knows she needs to work doubly hard to keep in step with young opponents who also boast of richer resources.

She starts training at 5:30 am at the Carpe Diem BJJ gym in Makati City, holds a class from 7 am to 8:30 am, trains again from 11 am to 1 pm and from 3 pm to 4 pm, and then teaches kids after all that.

But as committed as she is to jiu-jitsu, Custodio makes time to enjoy life, with wine and cheese among her guilty pleasures.

“After training, I’ll have a drink or some wine, but only at home. I don’t go out. And I make sure I’m asleep by 7 pm. It’s all about balance. It’s not just all about training — that’s one of the simple joys in my life. But I also make sure I pay for it. If I eat a lot of cheese and drink a lot of wine tonight, I make sure I make up for it with training the next day. I’ll make up for it with a really good training session every day,” said Custodio.

The work continues for Custodio as she eyes her first gold medal in the Asian Games, which will be staged in Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4.

After that, Custodio will consider whether to continue competing as she shifts her focus toward helping her students find success of their own.

“Whatever I’ve achieved, I want them to achieve it too. Because for some reason, when I win, I feel alright. But when my students win, the fulfillment is different. It makes me think I did something right,” she said.

Once dreaming of starting a family and having children, Custodio is convinced that jiu-jitsu is her purpose.

“I honestly never imagined that this would happen, that I would become a four-time world champion. This is my life now. Before, my goals in life were completely different: I wanted to get married, have children, and be a housewife. But when I got into jiu-jitsu, everything changed,” she said.

“My life really revolves around jiu-jitsu now because it feels like the only things I think about are how I can improve myself, improve my techniques, and improve the skills of our students.” – Rappler.com

World.title: The women of Cinemalaya
World.content:
IT’S A TIE. Marietta ‘Pokwang’ Subong (left) of ‘2 Valid IDs’ and Ruby Ruiz of ‘Status: Rejected’ share the Best Actress award at Cinemalaya 22.

Many have noted the excellent films in Cinemalaya 22, but what’s truly worth noting are the outstanding performances by women

“I have watched only two full-length films in competition at the Cinemalaya film festival. Mag-iina and A.ni.mal. But I pity the jury. Because the actors are so good! How will you rate them? Halimaw! Lamon! (Powerhouse performances!)”

Thus wrote multi-awarded film director Dwein Baltazar in Filipino on her social media account on August 12.

Mag-iina got the lion’s share of the Cinemalaya awards, including this year’s best film and outstanding direction, screenplay, production design, and musical score. A.ni.mal, on the other hand, received the Balanghai trophy for editing and supporting actress.

So many people who have been part of the independent film festival for many years as organizers, cast, and crew — and even the audience — have noted how excellent the films in this batch are.

But what’s truly worth noting are the outstanding performances by women.

Ruby Ruiz, Status: Rejected

Ruby Ruiz depicted the role of a lonely 69-year-old woman with an American dream in Status: Rejected.

“Not much preparation needed for this role because Biring is pretty much like Ruby,” quipped the veteran actress, who shared the Cinemalaya 22 Best Actress honors with Marietta “Pokwang” Subong.

“At 65, I realized that I yearn for more attention and affection from my children. When you feel that your relevance is diminishing, you amplify that to loneliness. I go through that now and am trying to cope with it.”

This is her fourth Cinemalaya win, having won Best Actress for Iska in 2019, and Best Supporting Actress for Ekstra in 2013 and Ginhawa in 2022.

“It was so much fun, and easy because [my co-actors were] all good, especially Alessandra de Rossi,” she replied. The other cast members are Beverly Salviejo and Yani Villarosa.

Marietta ‘Pokwang’ Subong (left) and Ruby Ruiz (top) hold their Cinemalaya 22 Best Actress trophies. Photos from CCP

Marietta ‘Pokwang’ Subong, 2 Valid IDs

Marietta “Pokwang” Subong starred in 2 Valid IDs as Sylvia, a woman desperate to obtain two identification cards to be able to claim a relative’s substantial remittance from overseas for her ailing husband Ramon (Joey Marquez).

Pokwang, who shared Best Actress with Ruby Ruiz, dedicated her award to all the Sylvias out there.

“Sa lahat ng pinagdadanasan po ng mga Pilipino. ‘Wag kayong mawalan ng pag-asa. Laban lang!” Pokwang said during her acceptance speech.

(To all Filipinos who are going through hardships, never lose hope. Just keep fighting!)

Pokwang won her first Cinemalaya award 10 years ago for her performance in Mercury is Mine.

“Alam ko mahirap ang buhay ngayon. Tipid-tipid. Pero andiyan kayo, sumusuporta. Pinatunayan ’nyong kaya natin ito. Bangon industriya. Kaya natin. Kaya ng Pilipino,” she said

(I know times are really hard. We’re all trying to make ends meet. But here you are, supporting us by watching our movie. You proved that we can ride this out. Let’s uplift the film industry. We can do it. We, Filipinos, can do this.)

Jackie Lou Blanco, Mag-iina

Jackie Lou Blanco, depicted the complicated and very difficult role of the matriarch of three generations of women “bound by grief, madness, and a dark family secret,” in the psychological horror film Mag-iina.

Jackie Lou Blanco (in black, second from left) with the cast of ‘Mag-Iina.’ Photo from CCP

Jackie Lou said Mag-iina came at the most demanding time of her career. Soon after finishing Anthropology for Barefoot Theatre Collaborative and the rerun of The Foxtrot, she multi-tasked a GMA teleserye and rehearsals for Virgin LabFest’s Lualhati while shooting Mag-iina.

“For the role itself —I play a much, much older woman, something I’ve never done before — the preparation was both physical and emotional,” Jackie Lou told Rappler.

“The prosthetics alone took hours and a lot of getting used to. Inaral ko talaga, dinama ko, ibinuhos ko lahat (I studied it thoroughly, felt it; gave it my all). I had to study not just how she moves and speaks, but how she carries a lifetime of being a mother. It was challenging, but so affirming.”

The veteran actress is now in the thick of rehearsals for the Hotdog band tribute musical Bongga Ka ‘Day.

Bituin Escalante, A.ni.mal

Interestingly, A.ni.mal was “written with each of the actors in mind,” revealed Cinemalaya 22 Best Supporting Actress Bituin Escalante.

Of her role as Dr. Grace Reyes — wife of the incumbent governor, and herself an aspiring governor — Bituin said, “Doc Grace is a woman born into privilege. A daughter of self-made politicians. She does not have the charm and political gifts of her parents. She just barely qualified as a doctor and did not even practice. “

“She married a charming, popular student-athlete she dated in college to continue their political stronghold in local politics. She feels the governorship is owed her,” she added.

Bituin Escalante with her husband and co-actor Reymund Domingo in ‘A.ni.mal.’ Photo by Ben Padero

To get into the role, “I had to find the whys for her actions by building a character profile; her history, her psychology and such. And all that lends to the approach to the script.”

In the film, Bituin worked with her real-life husband Reymund Domingo. “If felt like a safe place to work with him,” she said. “The most natural thing. Even if we’ve never fought the way they did.”

Maxine Ignacio, A.ni.mal

The reel and real daughter of acclaimed actress Frances Makil-Ignacio, Maxine Ignacio is a BA Theatre Arts alum of UP Diliman. She depicts the role of nepo baby Lily, who is supposed to be an animal rights advocate.

She had first read the role of Lily in a stage reading in 2024, and recalled having been “so excited to do it in whatever way, shape or form.”

“Lily is so complex and has so many layers,” Maxine said.

Maxine Ignacio with Anthony Falcon. Contributed photo

In any role that she plays, her goal is “to find the truth about the character,” answering questions such as “Who am I? Where am I? What is my relationship to my scene partners? What do I want to achieve? What do I do to get what I want?” or, basically, a shortened version of Uta Hagen’s Nine Questions.

“I did my homework by always going back to the script. [I] took down all the notes Direk Dustin [Celestino] would give during rehearsals and try to interpret it the best that I could,” she said.

Although she has worked with her mom twice before, this is the first time Maxine performed with her in a film as she debuts on screen.

“She trusts me as her co-actor, and treats me as an equal.”

Yayo Aguilla, Tayo Lang ang Nakakaalam

How did Yayo Aguilar prepare for the difficult role of the mom of an HIV positive patient (who also happens to be gay and have a partner) in Tayo Lang ang Nakakaalam?

“To establish the chemistry of the cast (Miguel Odron, Epy Quizon, and Martin del Rosario), we had a roundtable discussion, a script reading, and a look-test with our director (David Corpuz) and intimacy/acting coach the first time all four of us got together,” Yayo explained.

“We discussed the story, and each and every character. We rehearsed a few sequences that were crucial to the film.”

Yayo Aguila with Martin del Rosario on set. Contributed photo

“I had to immerse myself into the story,” said Yayo, who also shared she now has four adult children. “I had to put myself in the shoes of Gloria with a child (Bong) who is very, very ill, and he would be gone soon, and feel that he was really my son and not a fictional character.”

Yani Villarosa, Status: Rejected

Yani Villarosa said she’s happy and honored to have worked with the veteran actors on the set of Status: Rejected, including Ruby Ruiz and Alessandra de Rossi, as well as with “newer and younger collaborators.”

“They were so generous. I learned so much just by being there,” shared Yani, who plays Sophia, the granddaughter of Ruby’s character.

Yani Villarosa delivers in ‘Status: Rejected.’ Photo from Black Cap

Yani thinks it’s important for a younger person to be included in the script (she is of the same age as director and screenwriter Vahn Leinard Pascual, 26), seeing people their age as witnesses to generational patterns or pain of previous generations.

“Sophia is in that phase when she’s starting to understand the dynamics between her grandmother and mother, and this affects her as a person and as a woman,” she said.

Kat Hernandez, Para-paraan

Special Jury prize winner for the shorts category, Para-Paraan truly embodied the dictum of “show, don’t tell.” In it, we practically walk behind para powerlifter Katrina Hernandez, who goes around the metro using a wheelchair unaided as she ticks off three errands on her list.

Kat has a non-progressive condition called arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (AMC), and it was a two-woman production team for Hernandez and director Mae Chan Li — joint creators of Out of the Box, a platform “that uses storytelling, education, and public engagement to spark conversations about disability, accessibility and inclusion.”

“Winning this award means a lot to me, not just as recognition for the film, but as an opportunity to spark conversations about disability, accessibility, and inclusion,” Kat said.

Kat Hernandez with director Mae Chan Li. Photo from CCP

Alycia Avila, Hoy, Hoy, Ingat!

The youngest from this set of actresses is nine-year-old Alycia Avila of Hoy, Hoy, Ingat!, winner of the Audience Choice Award for Short Film.

Alycia, who plays the lead role Baby, was discovered by producer Alex Poblete while auditioning for the QCinema International Film Festival.

A fifth grader in a Paco public school, Alycia said she had fun on the set. Her only difficulty, she shared, was learning “Bisakol” or the Masbateño iteration of Bisaya.

“During the script reading, Direk Norvin (de los Santos) taught me and kuya VR Relosa (her co-actor) how to pronounce the words and what to stress in the conversations in the film” she said in Filipino. “I really tried to learn it and memorize it.”

Alycia Avila (center) of ‘Hoy, Hoy, Ingat!’ with director Norvin de los Santos and host Albert Sumaya. Photo from CCP

– Rappler.com

World.title: [Tech Thoughts] A Rappler conversation about creativity and AI assistance
World.content:
To what extent should one tag AI assistance they accept in creative work? We tackle the topic on Rappler's Everyday Tech chat channel.

Over on the Rappler Communities app’s Everyday Tech channel, our Friday morning conversation this week turned to a discussion about creativity and AI assistance.

Our discussion started off with a report that Apple Music was planning to add labels to songs made with AI. According to Billboard, Apple said any song tagged as being “materially generated using AI” by content providers, such as record labels and distributors, will have a visible label on the service.

Apple’s action follows a move to institute AI Transparency Tags, which requires content providers to disclose when and where AI is used in a “material” way — including artwork, track, composition, and music video composition.

Earlier in August, Spotify also introduced AI labels to its tracks — specifically an AI Persona badge on specific artists’ profiles. Meanwhile, Bandcamp banned AI use on its platform.

The conversation about AI and creativity made its way towards disclosing AI use for other creative pursuits. Gemma Mendoza, Rappler’s head of strategic programs, and I were discussing the sort of sliding scale of creativity and disclosure — between AI as a tool or an enabler.

For instance, does the use of an AI-powered grammar checker require a disclosure? How about using AI to help in formatting presentation slides?

I felt that the disclosure of AI use was important, but that maybe there should be a tiered approach to AI disclosure so as to distinguish between AI as a helper or tool versus AI taking over for the entire creative process.

For instance, Rappler has AI summaries, and for stories I handle or write, I also make sure the summaries are accurate. That said, I don’t treat the AI summary as my own words, even if I did write the story that created the AI summary.

Going back to the discussion of musicmaking, Gemma said that an issue worth discussing was whether an AI user would be shortcutting their way through music creation — or perhaps through other types of creative work.

“I think that at the end of the day — even if you used AI — the question would be similar to when you put your name on something. If it is crap, then you created crap,” she explained.

The conversation lasted about an hour, and there wasn’t anything definitive or life-changing about it, but it made me think more about my own prejudices against AI and using it. I’m still hesitant to use AI as I do prefer doing my own creative work, but it’s those kinds of discussions that broaden our worldviews just a little bit more, making these conversations worthwhile to have.

For those interested in joining a conversation, do download the Rappler app and in the Communities section, join the Everyday Tech chat channel. We have conversations from Monday to Friday at 10 am and 4 pm. We welcome new perspectives or ideas for topics to tackle next, aside from discussing the latest news about technology. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tokayev Says Vice President Appointment Expected Within 10 Days
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said the new Vice President is expected to be appointed within the next week or 10 days, speaking to media representatives after casting his ballot in the country’s first elections to the Kurultai on Aug. 23.

Responding to questions about the reforms and the changes expected after the Kurultai and the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi (People’s Council) begin their work, Tokayev described the newly established Vice President position as a significant and necessary institutional change.

“We deliberately established this new position in the Constitution. I would not be mistaken in saying that it is extremely necessary. In the current difficult times, such a position is particularly needed by our country,” Tokayev said.

He said the name of the person who will take the position is expected to become known within the next seven to 10 days, adding that it would be premature to disclose the candidate’s name during the voting process.

“I think this will be a well-known person whom you all know very well,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted the planned launch of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi, a new state body that he said would build on the work previously carried out by the Assembly of the People of Kazakhstan. According to him, the new institution will serve as a multifunctional political mechanism as part of the country’s broader reforms.

Tokayev on 2029 presidential election

Asked whether he intends to use his constitutional right to seek another presidential term in 2029, Tokayev said the Constitutional Court’s recent decision confirming his eligibility is lawful, but that discussing his future candidacy would be premature.

“The Constitutional Court made this decision. It is lawful, and I have the legal right to be re-elected. But as for the upcoming elections or, as you put it, whether I will run or not, and in which year, it is premature to speculate on this,” he said.

Tokayev said the government has many tasks to complete before it can address such questions. He also said the government’s composition would change, while stressing that there are currently no grounds for concern about its work.

“Personnel changes are always inevitable because they give the government new strength,” Tokayev said, adding that such changes should be aimed at providing a serious impetus to the government’s work rather than dismissals for their own sake.

Voter turnout exceeds 65.37%

Meanwhile, voter turnout in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai reached 65.37% by 4 p.m. on Aug. 23, with 8,240,336 voters having received ballots, according to the Central Election Commission (CEC).

The Kyzylorda Region recorded the highest turnout at 81.38%, followed by East Kazakhstan at 79.33%, Zhetisu Region at 77.03%, and Turkistan Region at 76.73%.

Turnout in the Aktobe Region stood at 75.63%, Akmola Region at 73.69%, Abai Region at 71.18%, Karagandy Region at 70.91% and Kostanai Region at 70.09%.

Among the cities of national significance, turnout reached 67.92% in Shymkent, 46.38% in Astana and 36.65% in Almaty.

Other regional figures were 67.23% in the Almaty Region, 67.06% in Pavlodar Region, 65.86% in Mangystau Region, 64.29% in Ulytau Region, 63.94% in North Kazakhstan, 63.37% in Atyrau Region, 61.81% in West Kazakhstan and 69.11% in the Zhambyl Region.

The CEC will provide the next update on voter turnout at 6 p.m.

World.title: International Observers Deliver Assessment of Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Vote
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s transition to a single-chamber legislature entered a new stage Aug. 23 as voters went to the polls to elect the country’s first Kurultai, with international observers monitoring the process.

The election is part of a broader effort to modernize Kazakhstan’s political institutions and strengthen their ability to respond to the country’s changing social and economic landscape, Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issetov said during an Aug. 22 briefing with foreign media.

He noted that Kazakhstan is pursuing political reform not because it is facing a crisis, but because the country is developing and its institutions should be prepared for the next stage of that development.

“We expect that the new political system will help maintain stability and continuity while ensuring the further development of state institutions. It should also provide more effective representation of public interests and improve the quality of decision-making,” Issetov said.

He also linked the reforms to the country’s economic development, saying a more complex economy requires more effective state institutions, predictable legislation and high-quality public administration.

“The more diverse society becomes, the more important it is to have mechanisms that allow for the various public interests to be taken into account. This is one of the main reasons behind the current constitutional reform,” Issetov said.

“It is not aimed at changing for the sake of change. Its objective is to bring political institutions in line with modern Kazakhstan and prepare them for the next stage of the country’s development,” he said.

The election has drawn international attention, with observers from foreign countries and organizations monitoring the electoral process, visiting polling stations and meeting with election officials and political parties. Their assessments offer an international perspective on how the new political system is taking shape in practice.

Shanghai Cooperation Organization

According to SCO Deputy Secretary-General T.R. Midhun, voting was well organized and polling stations were fully prepared.

“We went to the polling stations when they opened. We saw the procedures and the queues of people who were willing to participate in the election. It was early morning, and people were still very keen to start as early as possible,” he said.

Midhun noted that the mission’s task was to observe all stages of the electoral process and form an objective assessment based on direct observation and factual information. The mission will also monitor the closing of polling stations and procedures required under Kazakhstan’s legislation.

The SCO’s final assessment will be presented at a press conference on Aug. 24, he said.

In an interview with The Astana Times, Midhun said Kazakhstan’s political and economic reforms marked a profound transformation for the country.

“I think and hope that after these reforms Kazakhstan will strengthen its position and potential in the international arena. This, of course, will contribute to the SCO,” he said.

Midhun highlighted Kazakhstan’s role as a founding member of the SCO and praised its contributions in transport, logistics, political relations and cultural cooperation.

He also pointed to the country’s initiative to convene a meeting of heads of ports and logistics centers, calling it a “very constructive” contribution to the organization.

According to Midhun, SCO member states and dialogue partners account for around 40% of the world’s population and approximately one-quarter of global GDP.

“As one of the largest regional organizations, we have always paid special attention to the development of relations between countries in the fields of security, political relations, energy, and transport. When the world is changing, the role of the SCO is, of course, growing,” he said.

Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic Speaking Countries (TURKPA)

Osman Mesten, a Turkish lawmaker who chairs TURKPA’s Commission on Legal Affairs and International Relations, called the election a historic milestone.

“Following the referendum and the transition to a single-chamber legislature, the elections are the first held under the new system,” Mesten said.

Parliamentarians from Azerbaijan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Türkiye are participating in election observation missions.

Mesten noted that the delegation had met with the Central Election Commission chairman and representatives of political parties participating in the election.

“We observed that each party had been able to prepare for the elections and conduct outreach among voters to encourage participation and the exercise of their democratic rights,” he said.

He also highlighted women’s representation among candidates, noting that women account for around 43% of all candidates.

Mesten said Kazakhstan’s transition to a unicameral parliament could streamline the legislative process and improve its efficiency.

“A single-chamber legislature is certainly important from the perspective of democratic representation and for ensuring that the legislative process functions in a more orderly, efficient and effective manner,” he told The Astana Times.

Mesten noted that Türkiye had previously a bicameral legislature but transitioned to a unicameral parliamentary system following constitutional reforms.

“I believe that a single chamber enables decisions to be made more effectively, more quickly and more efficiently. It also eliminates some of the disadvantages associated with a dual-chamber system,” he said.

He also welcomed Kazakhstan’s decision to name the new legislature the Kurultai, describing the term as a reference to the country’s historical roots and shared heritage across the Turkic world.

“By choosing this name, Kazakhstan is referring to its deep historical roots. It also conveys the message that the country seeks to build a strong nation and a strong state by drawing strength from its heritage,” Mesten said.

“The name Kurultai is meaningful not only for Kazakhstan. It reflects our shared history and common roots. For this reason, it has inspired pride and enthusiasm throughout the Turkic world, including in Türkiye,” he said.

A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor Kazakhstan’s Kurultai election.

World.title: Kazakhstan Records 37.05% Voter Turnout by Noon in Kurultai Election
World.content:
ALMATY – Voter turnout in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai reached 37.05% as of noon on Aug. 23, with 4,670,816 voters having received ballots, according to the Central Election Commission (CEC).

Kyzylorda Region recorded the highest turnout at 47.59%, followed by Zhetisu Region at 47.29% and Turkistan Region at 43.14%. Turnout in the Aktobe Region stood at 42.5%, East Kazakhstan at 41.89%, Shymkent at 41.6% and the Karagandy Region at 40.56%.

The lowest turnout was recorded in Almaty at 17.87%. Other regions with turnout below 35% included the Mangystau Region at 34.68% and the Kostanai Region at 34.72%. Turnout in Astana reached 35.28%, while the Almaty Region recorded 39.05% and the Abai Region 38.51%.

Kazakhstan’s leadership votes

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev cast his ballot at polling station No. 520, located at the Palace of Independence in Astana. After voting, Tokayev briefed representatives of the media and described the election as a significant milestone for Kazakhstan, reported Akorda.

“Today is truly a historic day for our country. For the first time, we are holding elections to a unicameral Kurultai. This is an important historical event,” Tokayev said.

He noted that Kazakhstan has carried out large-scale reforms and achieved significant results, while emphasizing that substantial work remains.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov also cast his ballot in the first elections to the unicameral Kurultai, while Minister of Foreign Affairs Yermek Kosherbayev voted at polling station No. 514.

First Deputy Head of the Presidential Administration Erlan Karin voted at a polling station in Astana, describing the first Kurultai elections as a historic event for Kazakhstan.

Voting continues abroad

Polling stations for the Kurultai elections are operating now in more than 40 countries, allowing Kazakhstan citizens abroad to participate in the vote.

The election will elect 145 members of Kazakhstan’s new unicameral Parliament. Seven political parties are contesting the election under a proportional representation system in a single nationwide constituency, with a 5% threshold for entering the legislature.

The CEC will continue publishing voter turnout data every two hours throughout election day.

World.title: Kazakhstan Opens More Than 10,000 Polling Stations for First Kurultai Election
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan opened 10,363 polling stations across the country on Aug. 23 for Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai, according to the Central Election Commission (CEC).

Polling stations began operating at 7 a.m. Astana time, while 107 of them opened earlier at 6 a.m. based on decisions by territorial election commissions. In total, 12,605,788 citizens are included in the voter lists. Authorities also issued 17,132 absentee certificates, allowing voters to cast ballots outside their registered localities.

A total of 10,423 polling stations have been established for the election, including 79 stations in 61 foreign countries.

Voting abroad

Voting has also begun at polling stations abroad. Kazakhstan established 79 polling stations at diplomatic missions and consular offices in 61 countries to ensure citizens living abroad can exercise their constitutional right to vote. A total of 11,402 voters are registered at these stations.

According to Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issetov, 26 polling stations abroad had opened by 8 a.m. Astana time. Kazakh citizens in Tokyo and Seoul were the first to begin voting, at 3 a.m. Astana time.

As of 8 a.m., 228 citizens had cast their ballots at polling stations abroad.

Election rules

CEC member Lazzat Suyindik reminded voters and media representatives on Aug. 21. of restrictions on the publication of election-related opinion polls and forecasts. Under Kazakhstan’s election legislation, results of public opinion polls, forecasts of election results and other election-related research cannot be published during the five days preceding election day or on election day itself.

According to her, exit polls may be conducted on election day only outside polling station premises and by organizations that have notified the CEC in advance. Photographing or video recording a completed ballot and distributing such material is also prohibited on election day.

At the same time, voters are allowed to take photographs at polling stations, including near ballot boxes or while casting their ballots, provided that the photograph does not reveal which party they voted for. The restriction on distributing such images applies specifically to election day.

First Kurultai election

The election marks a new stage in Kazakhstan’s parliamentary system. Citizens will elect 145 members of the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral Parliament, through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency.

Seven political parties are contesting the election, with parties required to secure at least 5% of the vote to enter the legislature. A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor the election..

Starting at 10 a.m., the CEC will provide updates on voter turnout every two hours throughout election day.

World.title: S&P Upgrade Highlights Kazakhstan’s Economic Resilience and Investment Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – S&P Global Ratings raised Kazakhstan’s long- and short-term sovereign credit ratings on Aug. 21 to BBB/A-2 from BBB-/A-3, while maintaining a stable outlook. The agency also raised its transfer and convertibility assessment to BBB+ and affirmed Kazakhstan’s national scale rating at kzAAA.

The upgrade strengthens Kazakhstan’s position among investment-grade sovereigns and could improve investor confidence, according to the QZ Economy analytical Telegram channel.

“A higher sovereign rating is also an increase in confidence,” the experts said on Aug. 22, noting its potential to improve financing conditions for the economy, support Kazakh companies working with foreign creditors and investors, and strengthen Kazakhstan’s overall investment attractiveness.

Growth remains a key strength

The upgrade reflects what S&P describes as Kazakhstan’s “resilient GDP growth outlook as well as its ample external and fiscal buffers that could cushion future shocks.”

Preliminary data show GDP expanded 4.1% in January-June despite a sharp slowdown in the first quarter linked to disruptions in oil exports and production. S&P forecasts growth of 5.1% in 2026, moderating to 4-4.5% in 2027-2029.

The agency expects non-oil activity to partly offset the impact of fiscal consolidation and lower global oil prices. Construction and manufacturing have already provided additional momentum.

Buffers support fiscal consolidation

Kazakhstan’s government liquid assets are forecast to stabilize at around 21% of GDP over the next four years. The National Bank and government’s external assets exceed the country’s gross external debt, giving policymakers room to maneuver during external shocks.

Fiscal performance is also improving. The national budget deficit was 1.2% of GDP in the first half this year, on track toward the 2.5% full-year target. S&P expects the general government deficit to average 1.2-1.3% of GDP in 2026-2029, compared with 3.7% in 2025.

Tax revenue increased 17% year on year in the first half, including a 42% increase in VAT collection. Efforts to broaden the tax base and control spending are expected to support further consolidation.

Political analyst Gaziz Abishev linked the upgrade to the government’s fiscal and economic policy, including tax reform, expenditure controls and a stronger focus on developing processing industries.

“Financial discipline is what international experts like. The country is rationalizing spending and supporting accumulation, protecting the National Fund from being spent down,” Abishev said.

He also highlighted the government’s work with foreign investors and President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s economic pragmatism, which he said aims to maximize the benefits of cooperation with relevant partners while minimizing geopolitical risks.

Investment could become the key benefit

S&P expects investment to remain high at approximately 30% of GDP, driven by infrastructure, raw-material processing and energy projects. The investment program is central to Kazakhstan’s efforts to diversify its resource-driven economy.

The QZ Economy experts said the rating upgrade could strengthen confidence among foreign investors and international financial institutions, potentially “lower the cost of attracting financing for the economy” and improve conditions for Kazakh companies working with foreign creditors and investors.

The significance therefore extends beyond the sovereign balance sheet. A stronger rating can reduce perceived country risk, but its economic impact will depend on whether investment programs generate new production, infrastructure and long-term productivity.

Oil remains the main vulnerability

Kazakhstan remains exposed to commodity-price volatility and disruptions to oil exports. Nearly 80% of oil flows through the CPC pipeline via Russia, while oil accounts for more than half of exports.

S&P’s stable outlook assumes that possible CPC disruptions will be short-lived. A prolonged fall in global oil prices or extended pipeline disruptions could result in negative rating action. Conversely, stronger fiscal performance and a reduction in the government interest bill could support a positive rating action.

The upgrade is therefore both recognition and a benchmark for Kazakhstan. S&P’s stable outlook suggests that the country’s strong buffers will help it manage possible external shocks, while continued fiscal consolidation and diversification will remain important.

“S&P raised Kazakhstan’s rating even amid uncertainty in the global economy and volatility in commodity markets. This once again confirms that our economy can remain resilient in the face of external challenges. Reforms and hard work are already bearing fruit,” the QZ Economy analytical Telegram channel said.

The next test will be whether stronger sovereign credibility translates into lower financing costs, sustained investment and broader economic diversification.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Archaeological Heritage: From Ancient Steppe Discoveries to Shared Digital Atlas
World.content:
ASTANA — Archaeologists from across the Turkic world are moving towards a new model of cooperation that could make the region’s archaeological heritage easier to study as a single interconnected historical space.

At the third meeting of the Association of Research Institutes and Centers of Archaeology of the Turkic World (ARICA) in Bugac, Hungary on Aug. 15, experts discussed the creation of a shared digital infrastructure for archaeological research, reported the Turkic Academy. One of the key proposals is an electronic atlas of archaeological sites of the Turkic countries, which would bring together information on the location and chronology of archaeological sites, research findings, photographs, plans and scientific publications.

A digital information portal and electronic research database are also planned to facilitate the exchange of information on expeditions, research projects, publications, conferences, grants, educational programmes and specialists.

The initiative is substantial because archaeological heritage does not follow today’s political borders. Ancient settlements, burial grounds, trade routes and cultural traditions developed across territories that now belong to different states. A common digital research environment could therefore help scholars look at the history of Central Asia and the Eurasian steppe as a connected process rather than a collection of separate national histories.

Move toward practical cooperation

Founded in 2023, ARICA was created at the initiative of the Turkic Academy with the first meeting held in Shusha in 2024, followed by Ankara and Gaziantep in 2025. Kazakhstan’s Margulan Institute of Archaeology has been among its founding institutions. The association was created as a platform for joint research, exchange of experience and the development of cooperation among archaeological institutions of the Turkic world.

The Turkic Academy, headquartered in Astana, has played a coordinating role in this process, bringing together research institutions and specialists from across the Turkic world. ARICA meetings have involved archaeologists and academic institutions from Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Türkiye, Uzbekistan and Mongolia, among other countries.

The association’s agenda has gradually moved beyond institutional cooperation towards practical joint research. Proposed areas include joint expeditions, excavations and documentation of archaeological sites, as well as the study of Silk Road cities, early Turkic monuments, ancient irrigation systems, nomadic cultures and medieval production centers.

This gives Kazakhstan a role that goes beyond simply contributing archaeological sites to a future database. Kazakh institutions are themselves generating new archaeological data, developing international partnerships and contributing to projects designed to place the history of the Eurasian steppe in a broader regional context.

Kazakhstan’s vast array of archaeological evidence

For Kazakhstan, this is particularly relevant. The country occupies a vast part of the Eurasian steppe and contains archaeological evidence covering almost the entire history of human settlement in the region from the Stone Age and early metallurgy to the Kangju period, the Turkic era, the Oghuz world and the Golden Horde.

The scale of Kazakhstan’s archaeological record can be seen in discoveries made across the country in recent years. In 2025, the exhibition “New Discoveries in the Archaeology of Kazakhstan” presented finds covering the Stone Age, Eneolithic, Bronze Age, Saka-Sarmatian period and Middle Ages, reported the Ministry of Science and Higher Education. The exhibition also featured 3D reconstructions and digital models, demonstrating how traditional field archaeology is increasingly being combined with modern technologies.

One of the discoveries highlighted was the Tian Shan Aurignacian cultural tradition identified in southeastern Kazakhstan. The Stone Age finds provide new material for studying early human communities and technological development in Central Asia and their connections with broader prehistoric processes across Eurasia.

Another important discovery came from the Taisoygan complex in the Atyrau Region, where archaeologists uncovered an Eneolithic burial. The finds add to the archaeological record of western Kazakhstan and provide further evidence for the diversity of prehistoric communities that inhabited the territory of the country.

The Akmaya and Taldysai settlements in central Kazakhstan offer a different perspective. Copper ore and metallurgical remains found at the sites contribute to the understanding of ancient mining and metal production in Saryarka. Such evidence is important not only for reconstructing the economic life of ancient communities, but also for studying the development and spread of technological knowledge across the Eurasian steppe.

The Kangju period provides another important link between Kazakhstan and the wider history of Central Asia. Archaeologists working in the Turkistan Region have uncovered burial complexes and artefacts associated with the Kangju state, which existed from approximately the first century BC to the fourth century AD.

Among the finds was the burial of an elite warrior, accompanied by weapons, horse equipment, belt fittings and ornaments. The research has involved cooperation with international specialists, including researchers from Leiden University. Such projects demonstrate how archaeological sites in Kazakhstan can serve as platforms for international research into ancient Central Asian societies.

The Kangju archaeological record is particularly valuable because southern Kazakhstan was part of wider political, economic and cultural networks connecting Central Asia with neighbouring regions. Artefacts found at Kangju sites, including imported objects, provide evidence of long-distance contacts and cultural exchange.

Kazakhstan’s medieval heritage adds another layer to this historical picture. Zhankent, located in the lower Syr Darya region, is closely associated with the Oghuz world and is identified with the medieval center of the Oghuz Yabgu State. Archaeological research at the site continues to reveal information about urban life, architecture, craft production and the cultural environment of the medieval Syr Darya.

The site demonstrates why regional archaeological cooperation matters. The history of the Oghuz cannot be confined to a single modern country. Research into Zhankent can contribute to a broader understanding of the movement of people, goods, technologies and cultural practices across the Turkic world.

A more recent example comes from Zhantai in the Pavlodar Region. In 2026, archaeologists identified remains believed to be connected with an elite burial complex dating to the 14th–15th centuries. Researchers used lidar, ground-penetrating radar and 3D documentation to study the site, demonstrating how modern technologies can complement traditional excavation.

Why a shared atlas can matter

The discovery is particularly relevant to the proposed ARICA atlas because it illustrates how archaeological information can already be collected in highly detailed digital formats. Three-dimensional documentation can preserve the appearance and structure of archaeological features and make them available for further analysis by researchers who may not be able to visit the site themselves.

Today, archaeological information is often distributed among museums, universities, research institutes, expedition archives and scientific publications. Different institutions may use different formats, terminology and documentation systems. Important material can therefore remain difficult to locate even for specialists working on related historical periods. The ARICA initiative could help address this fragmentation.

A shared atlas would allow researchers to see archaeological sites in their geographical and chronological context. A scholar studying early Turkic settlements, for example, could compare sites across Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan, Mongolia, Türkiye and other parts of the Turkic world rather than examining each country’s archaeological record separately.

The database could also help identify connections between seemingly unrelated discoveries. Similar pottery, metalworking techniques, burial practices or architectural features could be traced across different territories. Such comparisons may help researchers develop new hypotheses about migration, trade, technological exchange and cultural interaction.

For international expeditions, the benefits could be practical as well. Researchers would have a clearer picture of which sites have already been studied, what publications are available, which projects are underway and which specialists have expertise in particular periods or research methods.

A shared database could also support heritage protection. Detailed records containing photographs, plans, geographic information and 3D documentation can help monitor archaeological sites, document their condition and preserve information about monuments that may be threatened by construction, natural processes or illegal excavations.

Kazakhstan’s efforts

The ARICA initiative comes at a time when Kazakhstan itself is developing its national system for archaeological research and heritage protection. According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Culture and Information, the country has 11,846 registered historical and cultural monuments, including 8,877 archaeological sites. The National Archaeological Service is being established on the basis of the Margulan Institute of Archaeology. Its work includes monitoring archaeological activities, providing scientific and methodological support, collecting research reports and developing a unified information system.

This national effort can complement the ARICA initiative. Kazakhstan’s own archaeological databases and documentation can provide a foundation for contributing verified information to a wider regional platform, while the international database can place individual Kazakh sites within a broader archaeological landscape.

The country is experimenting with digital approaches to heritage. In the Kyzylorda Region, for example, an interactive 3D map of historical and cultural heritage sites has been developed, while QR codes have been installed at a number of monuments.

International cooperation is also expanding. Kazakhstan’s Margulan Institute has developed partnerships with foreign archaeological institutions, including France’s National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research. Cooperation covers areas such as archaeology, research methods and the use of modern technologies.

Together, these developments indicate a broader transformation of Kazakhstan’s archaeological sector from isolated excavations towards systematic documentation, digitalisation, international research and long-term preservation.

World.title: How Tropical Greenhouse in Astana Quietly Changes Way You Think About Survival
World.content:
I had lived in Astana for years before I finally visited the greenhouse at the city’s Botanical Garden. Looking back, I’m not entirely sure why it took me so long. I’d walked through the park countless times, watched runners weave between its paths, admired the flower beds in summer and the endless white snow in winter, yet somehow I had never stepped inside the greenhouse. Maybe that’s because from the outside it doesn’t prepare you for what’s waiting behind the glass.

The moment the doors close, Astana disappears. The dry steppe air gives way to warm humidity. The scent of wet soil replaces the smell of asphalt. Palm leaves stretch above your head, citrus trees are heavy with fruit, papayas quietly ripen in one corner, coffee berries turn bright red in another, and for a second your brain struggles to reconcile what your eyes are seeing. You are still standing in one of the coldest capitals in the world, yet everything around you belongs somewhere thousands of kilometers to the south. It feels almost impossible.

The Astana Botanical Garden officially opened in 2018 as part of the celebrations marking the capital’s twentieth anniversary. Scientists from Kazakhstan worked alongside colleagues from Germany, Italy, France and several CIS countries to create what has become not only a public attraction but also an important scientific collection dedicated to preserving plant biodiversity.

That scientific mission is exactly what brought me to Laila Zekenova, the head of the greenhouse, who has spent years looking after hundreds of species that have somehow learned to call Astana home.
