World.title: Iran president says nation has 'many problems' due to sanctions
World.content:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian admits his country's citizens face "many problems", after the United States launched a new wave of sanctions seeking to further isolate its economy.

"I understand we have many problems in society right now. We are trying to prevent these as much as we can," Mr Pezeshkian said in a speech broadcast on state television on Sunday.

His comments came after the US vowed last week to bring about the "collapse" of the Iranian regime through a newly announced sanctions campaign, nearly six months after the start of their war.

In his response, Mr Pezeshkian said that, because of US President Donald Trump, Iran was "in a full-scale economic, military and security war".

People at the Grand Bazaar in Tehran where prices are likely to rise due to sanctions. (Reuters: Majid Asgaripour/WANA)

"He says he is imposing the most crushing and terrifying sanctions on Iran," Mr Pezeshkian said.

The Iranian government has faced several waves of mass protest in recent years.

Iranians describe life under regime Three Iranians have shared their insights on life under the regime, as the war passes its fifth month.

They have often been triggered by economic hardships, including inflation and exchange rate swings, leading to declining purchasing power.

At the end of last year, a protest movement initially sparked by the rising cost of living turned into mass demonstrations denouncing those in power.

Authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths during the unrest, accusing the US and Israel of orchestrating the violence.

Foreign-based NGOs, however, said officials had launched an indiscriminate crackdown that left thousands dead.

Scott Bessent will go into detail about the new sanctions against Iran on Monday. (AP: Matt Rourke)

"We are striving with all our hearts to overcome inflation, livelihood problems, unemployment, and to secure the future of the people, so that they can live with dignity and pride," Mr Pezeshkian said on Sunday.

Since the war began on February 28, 3,636 people have reportedly died in Iran, with 2,100 estimated to be civilian deaths.

On Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will host a media conference to outline the exact details of the economic measures to be imposed on Iran.

AFP/ABC

World.title: Sydney shark attack victim reflects on 'second chance at life'
World.content:
Sydney shark attack victim Leah Stewart says she has not fully recovered more than two months after the incident, but feels like she has been given a "second chance at life".

Ms Stewart's family had previously provided updates on her condition on a fundraising site. On Sunday she wrote for the first time about her experience.

"After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I'm so happy that I've progressed enough to build some independence, and I can finally see some light after all of this," she said.

" I want you to know that I feel like I've been given a second chance at life, and I'm not going to waste it. "

Leah Stewart says the past few months have been "incredibly difficult". (Supplied: Stewart family)

On June 13, Ms Stewart was taken to St Vincent's Hospital in a critical condition after being mauled by a white shark while she was out for a morning swim, between the flags and close to the shore, at Coogee Beach in Sydney's east.

The 35-year-old was bitten on her leg and arms, suffered multiple fractures throughout her body and lost a lot of blood.

She was in an induced coma for days and underwent multiple surgeries, including the amputation of one of her arms.

'My recovery has been remarkable'

The mother-of-one said she has been focusing on her healing and doing everything in her "power to get back to some sort of normal life".

"I still have a long way to go, but my recovery has been remarkable."

More than $500,000 has been raised to aid her recuperation, and while Ms Stewart profusely thanked the community for its generosity, she said it was time to "turn off donations".

"Because what you've offered has given us enough to recover, to stay in our home, and to give us options for further medical treatment down the road," she said.

Leah Stewart says the support she has received has "inspired me to get better, not bitter". (Supplied: Stewart family)

She added the support she had received locally and from all over the world had contributed to her recovery.

" You've inspired me to get better, not bitter. "

About 11 days after the attack, the 35-year-old teacher spoke to her family for the first time after she was briefly woken from an induced coma.

Her first words, at the time, to her husband and mother were "I love you".

"Her first thoughts were with her daughter, August, and wanted to check she was OK," Ms Stewart's brother said.

NSW has experienced a number of shark-related incidents this year.

In January, 12-year-old Nico Antic died in hospital after he was attacked at Vaucluse.

Later that month, musician Andre de Ruyter lost his leg after he was bitten by a suspected bull shark at Manly Beach.

The attacks have led to an expansion of a drone surveillance program, which now covers 72 beaches along the NSW coast from dawn to dusk.

World.title: Trump hits back at Canada after retaliatory tariffs announced
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has hit back at Canada after Prime Minister Mark Carney announced retaliatory tariffs on the United States following a breakdown in trade negotiations.

"Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!" Mr Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

"They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!" he said.

Since beginning his second term, Mr Trump has made numerous references to making Canada the "51st state" of America, which has infuriated the northern neighbours.

Earlier, Mr Carney said that new Canadian tariffs would take effect on September 8, notably targeting the US steel and dairy industries.

New 50 per cent US tariffs impacting about $US20 billion ($28 billion) worth of goods, or 5.5 per cent of Canadian exports to the US, came into force on Saturday.

Canadian and US steel products will be impacted by the tit-for-tat tariffs. (AP: Nick Iwanyshyn/The Canadian Press)

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, electronics and other products mark a further worsening of relations between the longtime allies and major trading partners.

The two countries failed to reach a trade deal late on Friday, with each side blaming the other for derailing three days of intensive negotiations.

The breakdown complicates the future of a US-Mexico-Canada free-trade pact.

Mr Trump's new tariffs hit sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment,

These duties do not exempt Canadian products under the three-nation trade deal, which has shielded most Canadian exports to the US in the past 18 months.

A frosty relationship between Mark Carney (left) and Donald Trump (right) has hit a new low over tariffs. (AP: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press, File)

The new US tariffs cover around 5 per cent of Canada's exports to the US.

They could expose some vulnerable industries such as softwood lumber and wine to severe damage and lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts have said.

PM says Trump considering tariff exemption Anthony Albanese says he has urged Donald Trump to consider giving Australia a full exemption from Washington's sweeping tariffs.

"We will be mobilising our network of businesses in all regions and all sectors to brace for impact and make the best of a bad situation," said Candace Laing, CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of the most vocal opponents of US tariffs, supported Mr Carney's decision to retaliate.

"I'm glad he didn't sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector, and the manufacturing sector," Mr Ford said.

There were also US proposals that affected Canadian culture, language and sovereignty, Mr Carney said, without elaborating.

He was elected last year on a promise to be a tough negotiator with Mr Trump, and remains broadly popular. Polls show most Canadians oppose making any concessions to the US.

"Canadians must stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses," Pierre Poilievre, the leader of the official opposition Conservative Party, said in a statement.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Immersive experiences at heart of Powerhouse Parramatta grand opening
World.content:
A crystal tunnel set within a meteorite, a maze of mirrors and a vintage Qantas plane will be among the exhibits on offer when Powerhouse Parramatta opens its doors on November 7.

The full program for the museum's grand opening was revealed on Sunday, with work continuing to install more than 3,000 objects sourced from Australia and around the world.

The museum is promising an immersive experience, including an exhibition of five major works by British artist Es Devlin.

The Turning includes a labyrinth of mirrors called the Forest of Us.

The Forest of Us artwork involves a labyrinth of mirrors. (Supplied: Andrea Mora)

Visitors will be encouraged to get lost in its light-filled maze, while discovering the "striking visual symmetries" between trees and human lungs.

Powerhouse CEO Lisa Havilah said one of the "beautiful things" about the new space at Parramatta was its flexibility, allowing for large-scale installations.

"We're able to create these exhibitions that people will really be able to immerse themselves in," Ms Havilah said.

" It's also about presenting the collection in new ways as well. "

Devlin's Memory Palace will also feature in the exhibition. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Devlin's other works include Memory Palace, an immersive 3D cityscape, and Collective Portrait, which will invite visitors to draw portraits of strangers.

'Don't be scared' of the dark

An immersive experience catering to children will be an exhibition called The Dark.

"The Dark can be wondrous. There's no need to be scared," the museum's program teases.

The Dark is among the exhibitions catering to children. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Ms Havilah said the exhibition would be set inside a meteorite-like installation, showcasing more than 800 objects including an impressive minerals collection.

"There's a crystal tunnel, there are objects that make noise.

"There are different perspectives of how you imagine the dark, whether it's deep into space, deep underwater or deep in your body."

The Dark will also display the cherished personal objects of children from across Western Sydney.

"We did a call-out and 100 kids … have loaned us their most special object," Ms Havilah said.

"So there's a whole room with these 100 objects, but also the stories behind each of [them]."

One room will feature the favourite objects from 100 children across Western Sydney. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Walking on water

The third of the new exhibitions announced is a First Nations-led work called Overflow.

Through the films of acclaimed director and Kamilaroi man Ivan Sen, visitors can learn about Aboriginal custodianship of the oceans, rivers and other waterways in NSW.

According to the Powerhouse, Overflow will shine a light on cultural practices that foster species protection, flood mitigation, sustainable and commercial fishing and water quality.

Films by Kamilaroi man Ivan Sen are part of the Overflow exhibition. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta )

Ms Havilah said audiences would be invited to "walk on water" as part of the exhibition.

"There will be a huge platform in the middle of the space that will have water in the middle of it," she said.

There will be five opening exhibitions, two of which were previously announced.

Task Eternal will explore the "human ambition to defy gravity", and the display will include a NASA moon rock and original drawings of flying machines by Leonardo da Vinci.

It will also feature the Avro 504K— a replica of the very first Qantas plane.

A replica of the very first Qantas plane will be on display when the museum opens. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta )

Another exhibition, The Mall, will span two storeys of the Powerhouse, exploring the history and evolution of the modern shopping centre.

Western Sydney will get another nod in this exhibition, as the birthplace of the Westfield shopping centre — a concept that was exported to the world.

Rare items from Australian fashion brands will be on show, along with the signature jeans worn by Apple co-founder Steve Jobs.

The display will also include prototypes of the Predator boot, conceived by Australian footballer Craig Johnston and worn by David Beckham.

The Mall will be exhibited over two storeys of the museum. (Supplied: Jo Duck)

Kids see it for free

All of the exhibitions will be free of charge for visitors under 16 years of age.

However, Task Eternal will attract an as-yet undisclosed entry fee for visitors who are 16 years old and over.

Powerhouse Parramatta opening date revealed The NSW government announced in May that construction of the $915 million museum had been completed four years after work began.

Ms Havilah said the museum was designed to increase Sydneysiders' access to "world-class arts and culture."

"It's a really great gift," she said.

"To have four of the five exhibitions free to the public, I think is incredible."

Arts Minister John Graham said the $915 million project, which also includes storage and archiving, would offer good value to families facing cost-of-living pressures.

"We want to ensure that price isn't a barrier for young people to explore the big ideas, the creativity, the innovation that Powerhouse Parramatta will exhibit and celebrate," he said.

World.title: Quick hits: A Shoriful stunner amid more left-arm carnage in the 29th two-day Test
World.content:
Mitchell Starc delivers once more but it's another left-arm seamer who delivers the ball of the series, as Test cricket is blessed with its 29th two-day match.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Shoriful's ball of the series

Cameron Green was felled by a brutal inswinging yorker. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

It wouldn't have taken a rocket scientist to determine that Cam Green held the key for Australia at the start of day two.

The towering all-rounder, buoyed by his drought-breaking ton in Darwin, was once again looking precisely the player he had for so long promised to be.

With Green well set on 67 and clattering boundaries to either side of the wicket, it was going to take something special to remove the big man.

And Shoriful Islam, having already ripped through Australia's middle order late on day two, delivered something very, very special.

The left-armer's pinpoint yorker swung in late and dramatically, with Green falling over himself in a futile attempt to keep it out.

The ball thudded into the Australian's big toe on its way past the stumps and, after a brief consultation with DRS, was given out LBW to what was surely the ball of the series.

And that wasn't the end of the story for left-arm seamers on day two …

2. Starc continues the left-arm carnage

Mitchell Starc picked up from where he left off in the second innings. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Shoriful, who was almost inconceivably yanked from the bowling attack after that stunner against Green, ended the innings with figures of 7-48, the best-ever return for a Bangladeshi bowler while playing away from home.

Combine that with the 6-12 Mitchell Starc plundered early on day one, and left-arm seam had returned overall figures of 13-60, while accounting for 13 of the 20 wickets to fall in the match.

And it wasn't long before those numbers were improved even further.

He couldn't manage a wicket in his first set, but Starc struck with his eighth delivery of the innings, extracting some extra bounce to have Shadman Islam caught off a leading edge at point.

And the very next ball, Starc had his eighth of the match, having kissed the top of Mominul Haque's off stump with the Bangladeshi attempting an ill-advised leave.

An almost-customary double strike from Australia's supreme new-ball destroyer.

Starc eventually finished with figures of 4-39 for the innings and, with 10-51, the second-best match figures of his career.

3. Smith takes a screamer after tea

Tailender Taskin Ahmed had set himself well in the lead-up to the tea break, but he fell at the very first hurdle in the evening session.

Lyon's first delivery was a beauty, pitching and turning away from the leftie, who swung hard and found a healthy outside edge.

And Steve Smith, in place at his familiar position at slip, had to have his wits about him to complete a very good one-handed grab.

He's Test cricket's most prolific catcher for a reason, after all.

Taskin, who had provided perhaps Bangladesh's brightest spot in an otherwise pitch-black innings in swatting a massive six over long on in the shadows of tea, was out for 7.

4. The shortest session ever?

With Shoriful in at No. 11, the end was very clearly nigh in Mackay.

However, Shoriful showed in the first innings that he had at least some ability with the bat, top scoring with a rather frenetic 14 from 19 deliveries.

He survived the first ball of his second dig, defending Lyon out into the off side.

But it was all over with the very next ball.

Shoriful had a big swing at one, caught a thick outside edge and ballooned a dolly out to Starc at point, with Australia's superlative spearhead fittingly bringing the match to an end.

With two wickets falling in just three balls, it had to be close to the shortest non-weather-affected session in Test history.

5. The 29th two-day Test

Australia cruised to victory within two days. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

There have been 2,632 Test matches played in cricket's lengthy red-ball history, with 457 of them held in Australia.

As of today, there have been just 29 finish inside two days.

Only five of those have happened in Australia.

And yet, in the last 20 Tests that have been played on these shores, it has happened four times.

Australia thumped South Africa on a Gabba green top in 2022, and then there were two, two-day Tests during last summer's Ashes, one in Perth and the other at the MCG.

The only Australia-hosted Test to finish inside two days before that game in Brisbane four years ago took place in Melbourne against the West Indies, in February 1931.

Eleven of the two-day Tests in history took place before World War I (between 1882 and 1912), a further three either side of World War II (1931-1946) but then none between 1946 and 1999.

Then, since 2000, there have been 13 two-day Tests. The cost of a fast-paced world, perhaps.

World.title: Swans AFLW captain says support 'just unbelievable' as record smashed
World.content:
Sydney AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy wasn't sure what to expect for her side when they ran out for the first instalment of a historic double-header at the SCG.

The Swans dominated headlines across the country all week, filling both front and back pages of every newspaper, for a scandal that called the club's culture into question.

Swans fans descend on SCG amid club scandal Sydney Swans fans react to an emotional week, where a scandal continues to engulf the club, as they prepare to watch a historic double header at the SCG.

What the women's team got was an outpouring of support which broke the side's attendance record with 16,672 fans filling the stands to watch them play.

That is more than double the previous club record of 8,264.

"It's amazing. We weren't sure what we were going to expect this week, but to see the support that we've received today is just unbelievable," McEvoy told Fox Footy after the game.

"The members and fans are so tight and they know that we're united as a club and we're better than what we were at the start of the week.

The Swans doubled its crowd attendance record. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

"I'm just so grateful to have the support that we had today and the girls were able to turn it on.

"We had a few nervous girls, that's for sure, but we absolutely turned it on."

The scenes were particularly celebratory on the ground post-siren, after Sydney beat Essendon by 24 points.

It was just the second time the women have played on the SCG for premiership points and the first in a double billing with the men's.

Loading Instagram content

Before locking in to warm up, star men's players Errol Gulden and captain Callum Mills got around the women's players.

Gulden was also seen going up to the crowd giving the fans a big thank you for turning out in droves.

Some of those fans left before the men's game, as a boycott had been suggested in the days before the match as a scandal continues to engulf the club.

It's unclear how many fans left in protest to the scandal, but a steady stream was seen leaving.

Swans players spent time with fans after the game. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Swans fans cheer from the stands. (Getty: Darrian Traynor/AFL Photos)

Lulu Clarke, who has been a Sydney Swans fan for as long as she can remember, was one of the fans who walked out.

Ms Clarke had bought a ticket to the men's game, unaware the women were also playing, but once the news broke of the incident she knew she would not be staying for both games.

"Of late, I've definitely drifted apart from the Swans and the AFL industry as a whole," Ms Clarke said.

"I decided that I'm absolutely not going to the men's game, even if those five players were still stood down. There's no way I could just show up and watch it. It just didn't sit right with me."

Former Matilda Sarah Walsh also left the stadium after the women's game, saying it had been a "tough week", but stressed she was not boycotting the men's team.

"It's not a new story but I have a five-year-old daughter who I brought here today to support the women's team," Ms Walsh said.

"I think you can have a club and not expect someone to be a fan of both teams.

"I think that's the nuance of sport, don't expect Socceroos fans to be Matildas fans … We've got a long way to go in society. I don't think this is a Sydney Swans issue at all … it's a societal issue and we all need to do better."

Swans fans Kayley and Georgia went to the SCG to support the AFLW side. (ABC)

Swans fans Kayley and Georgia told ABC News they were there to support the women and will likely just watch a bit of the men's game.

"It's very disappointing from the men's team … I feel like we were very disappointed in everything that happened," Georgia said.

Kayley said the situation was upsetting.

"We've been supporting the Swans since we were kids as well. So, it was just shocking," she said.

"We never thought that any players from this team could do something like this. It was really upsetting."

Many fans held signs during the game along the lines of "I'm here for AFLW".

World.title: Thousands line riverbank to welcome Spirit IV 'home' to Devonport
World.content:
After years of delays and cost overruns, there was cause for celebration in Devonport today as one of the two new Bass Strait ferries arrived at its home port for the first time.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff was among the crowd welcoming Spirit of Tasmania IV to the north-west coast.

"I was here around 7am and I was with thousands of other Tasmanians … people of all ages," Mr Rockliff told reporters.

"I got the real sense there that this was a dawn of a new era for tourism, for freight, for Tasmania.

"And the sense of occasion was most certainly there.

"People were excited and people were very proud as they could see their ship, Spirit IV, sail up the river, turn on a dime and back in perfectly to the gantry."

Premier Jeremy Rockliff and TT-Line chair Ken Kanofski welcomed Spirit of Tasmania IV to Devonport. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Crowds gathered to watch Spirit of Tasmania IV arrive at its home port for the first time. (ABC News)

But it has not been all smooth sailing to get to this point.

Spirit IV, and its sister ship Spirit V, were initially planned to be ready for service in 2021.

But the ferry replacement program has been beset by delays and cost blowouts relating to both the ships themselves and the wharf infrastructure needed to accommodate them.

In May, state parliament's Public Accounts Committee heard the program, which started in 2018, had cost $717 million more than was forecast in the original business case.

Spirit of Tasmania IV was stored in Scotland before leaving Europe for Australia. (Supplied: TT-Line)

Most of the cost overrun related to the new berth at Devonport.

"You can always look back," Mr Rockliff said today.

"But this is about looking forward … and big projects like this have their challenges, there's no doubt about that.

"But big projects are here for the next generation, the next three decades or more.

"They are the projects that are worth the investment, they're worth the blood, sweat and tears because they always deliver."

Loading...

One of those in the crowd, Rodney Winwood, said "it was nice to see" the ship arrive.

"I had my doubts whether it would fit, but I think a lot of people are here to see whether it would fit really," he said.

Rodney Winwood was among the crowd to see the ship arrive. (ABC News)

Two days of testing

Ferry operator TT-Line's chair, Ken Kanofski, said Spirit IV would be in Devonport until tomorrow afternoon, with its hydraulics, loading systems and the management systems set to be tested.

"The purpose is really to test the gantry and the ship together in a live environment," Mr Kanofski said.

Ken Kanofski says Spirit IV is undergoing two days of testing in Devonport. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

"We've been doing it in Geelong with both ships for a number of times now.

"The gantries are built to designs, clearly, but you want to fine tune the systems, bring the two together for the first time," he said.

Spirit IV will return to Victoria following the testing.

"We'll also bring Spirit V here in September in order to undertake testing of Spirit V with the gantry as well," Mr Kanofski said.

Mr Kanofski said the new ships were still on track to start ferrying passengers in October.

People lined the Mersey River to see the ship arrive. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Emotion and nostalgia on banks of Mersey

Tasmania's Infrastructure Minister Kerry Vincent said there was celebration and nostalgia among the crowd gathered on the banks of Devonport's Mersey River to see the new ship arrive.

"A lot of emotion. There's a lot of old people here that … could remember the Princess and the Empress all talking about the changes and how important these new ships would be for Tasmania," he said.

The Princess of Tasmania and later the Empress of Australia connected Tasmania with Victoria from 1959 until TT-Line's Abel Tasman took over the route in 1985.

The cafeteria on board Spirit of Tasmania IV. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Mr Rockliff said during his first year in politics, he saw Spirits I and II arrive in Tasmania.

"That was also controversial at the time, and I think I might have even broken away from my team at the time as a candidate and supported the two new ferries when our side of politics didn't," he said.

"[To] 24 years later to see brand new ships … and these are purpose-built, brand new for Tasmania and Tasmanians, it's a very proud [moment]."

The ship's arrival has been labelled the "dawn of a new era" by the premier. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Devonport Mayor Alison Jarman said the new ship would be the city's "shining light".

She said there was a sense of celebration around town.

"We're getting hugs, we're getting high fives, we're getting people shaking our hands and congratulating us. And we're just saying to them, 'now, just tell everybody we're ready to go'," Councillor Jarman said.

World.title: Dutch F1 Grand Prix live: Piastri out to make history among the Zandvoort dunes
World.content:
Oscar Piastri found plenty of encouraging pace, but it still wasn’t enough to get McLaren’s Australian ace into the qualifying shake-up at Zandvoort as teammate Lando Norris roared to back-to-back poles at the Dutch Grand Prix.

Back at the track where this time last year he had seemed to be on top of the world, Piastri had looked sharp for most of the qualifying session on Saturday, hours after he had only been able to finish fifth in the sprint race behind victorious Mercedes driver George Russell.

Lando Norris waves to the crowd from the drivers’ parade ahead of the 2026 Dutch F1 Grand Prix. Getty Images

But when it came to the third and final qualifying session with spots of rain threatening, it was Norris who continued his resurgence, taking pole just as he had done last time out at the Hungarian Grand Prix when he went on to win the race.

It left Norris chuckling: “Our car is certainly the best in high speed, no doubt -- or I have the biggest balls. ... I don’t know!”

World.title: Swans crisis deepens as fresh allegations of ‘multiple sexual assaults’ emerge
World.content:
At least one fresh allegation of sexual assault and multiple claims of sexual conduct without consent have been made by the three women at the centre of an investigation involving Sydney Swans players at the Pullman East Melbourne. They come as police were alerted to the potential existence of a recording relating to the events at the hotel in the early hours of last Monday. The Pullman hotel in East Melbourne, where the Sydney Swans players stayed. Simon Schluter The new allegation from the woman represented by Jackson Pannam of Slater & Gordon, is that she was the victim of “multiple sexual assaults”. Allegations against multiple men



The other two women are being represented by firm Carbone Lawyers. Multiple sources close to those women with knowledge of the matter, but not authorised to speak publicly, told this masthead they had alleged to police that they were subjected to conduct of a sexual nature beyond what was agreed to with multiple men when they were engaged as topless waitresses. The statements will form part of the police investigations into potential criminal conduct. The three women were engaged for the players and their friends during a night of partying following the team’s victory over Essendon at the MCG in round 23. Slater & Gordon said the sexual assaults alleged by its client were reported to Victoria Police, who have maintained to date they are investigating “a report of a sexual assault”. When asked specifically by this masthead on Sunday whether the investigation was broadened to include two of the women’s separate allegations of sexual conduct without consent, a Victoria Police spokesperson said, “we have nothing further to add”. This masthead is not suggesting that any of the men in the room engaged in conduct of a sexual nature without consent, only that it has been alleged.



“We are not providing ongoing commentary around this investigation,” a police spokeswoman said. A reported recording Two AFL industry sources, who wished to remain anonymous, confirmed that the Swans passed details of the potential recording to the police via the AFL after a person contacted the club claiming to have information that could be relevant to the investigation. This masthead does not claim to know whether the recording exists or what information it may contain, only that a person contacted the club about its existence before their details were referred to police. Swans players (from left) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Artwork: Marija Ercegovac



The Swans have confirmed five of their players – Issac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon – were in the hotel room in the early hours of August 17. The players have been banned by their club for breaching its behavioural standards, for which they apologised. But a source with knowledge of the situation has previously told this masthead that the players deny any criminal wrongdoing. Other men, including recently retired Swans player Taylor Adams, were also in the room. Adams has not responded to requests for comment by this masthead. It is not clear which men the allegations are about. The AFL integrity unit steps back from making inquiries about such matters to let the police investigation run its course. Police have not yet interviewed the five suspended players. Each of the women last week made statements to Victoria Police outlining their version of events. Victoria Police on Saturday confirmed its investigation was continuing.

AFL 2026 ‘No culture is perfect’: Swans launch a review into late-night party that rocked the club “Detectives from the sexual crimes squad continue to investigate a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne on 17 August,” a police statement read. “The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established and a number of people have been spoken to.” The police investigation Carbone Lawyers said on Friday that it was preparing to launch legal action in the Supreme Court of Victoria against the five players and the club.



The lawyer representing the two women who alleged sexual conduct without consent told this masthead that the legal proceedings would be launched in the Common Law Division of the Victorian Supreme Court, with the women set to claim damages for pain and suffering, psychological injury and economic loss. Related Article Opinion

Gender equality From the Swans to Scots: Blaming the alleged victim means a harrowing truth can be avoided Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist “We are currently investigating the circumstances and preparing to commence legal proceedings against the club and potentially the individuals involved,” Manny Carbone, a partner at Carbone Lawyers, said. “Our clients are extremely traumatised and feel that their dignity and personal rights have been seriously violated by the events of Monday.” The Swans have denied there were any other club officials or staff members in the hotel room.



This masthead has previously reported that two sources familiar with the police investigation, but not authorised to speak publicly, confirmed drugs were involved in the early morning incident. However, both said the Swans teammates had denied being responsible for the drugs being there or taking them. World.title: Boning up on geography
World.content:
“Ah, Girilambone (C8),” effuses Bob Edgar of Moss Vale. “Nice choice, Janice Creenaune. I hope you have time for a delightful round trip via Gulargambone, Quambone and Billybingbone.”

“Letters to newspapers claiming the first sighting of magpies (C8) and blowflies are older than Granny,” reckons the canny Phil Kanaley of Glebe. “PG Wodehouse observed that ‘Nobody knows why, but editors have a weak spot for cuckoos, and anyone who hears the first one is pretty sure of an entree to their columns … what is known in my profession as ‘cuckoo-work’ … there is no market whatever for the second man who hears the cuckoo.’ At that time Granny was but a lass, not making her debut until 1947, but has since endured 79 summers of ornitho/entomo-logical encounters of the first kind.”

Edward Loong of Milsons Point reports that “not just one but three separate magpies were dive-bombing this morning adjacent to Wendy Whiteley’s Secret Garden at Lavender Bay, so I’m told by one of Wendy’s gardeners. He should know – being the target of all three. Unlike past years, I was spared – but fingers crossed for my morrows after.”

“The recent reference to the Edinburgh Writers’ Festival in the Herald reminded me of when we saw Terry Jones of Monty Python fame there many years ago,” says Nola Tucker of Kiama. “I bought his book and asked if he could dedicate it to my grandchildren. ‘Yes’, he replied, pen poised, ‘what are their names?’ ‘Just make it to the grandchildren as there are nine.’ Yes...’ very patiently ‘and what are their names?’ So I told him and still have the book with the nine grandchildren’s names neatly inscribed and his signature under them. Later on, we had a tenth grandchild, but I didn’t go back.”

Sometimes, a strict dress code (C8) can be a nice little earner. Here’s Paul Keys of Clouds Creek: “At the Hornsby Police Boys’ dance in the mid-’60s, the requirement was to wear socks, which could be purchased there. They also had some great bands playing.”

World.title: Swans’ AFLW team ride support for win; Magpies battling; Carlton on song
World.content:
Forward Nell Morris-Dalton has shown Carlton selectors that they made a worthwhile decision to salvage her AFLW career, as she dazzled in a 27-point victory over Adelaide.

Morris-Dalton booted three goals for the Blues (2-0) at Ikon Park to help last year’s preliminary finalists remain undefeated with a 7.8 (50) to 3.5 (23) win.

Carlton’s Nell Morris-Dalton. Getty Images

The performance comes after she was delisted by Collingwood at the end of last season and missed the initial cut for Carlton’s top-flight team after moving to their VFLW side.

But the 25-year-old was handed a lifeline when midfielder Maddy Guerin ruptured her ACL and on Sunday the injury replacement showed coach Mathew Buck that she deserves to be a mainstay.

World.title: Demons accused of wage theft and probity breaches by former CEO
World.content:
The former chief executive of the Melbourne Demons has claimed he was dismissed after raising concerns about widespread underpayment of administrative staff and complaining about the club’s use of a consultancy firm linked to former premier Daniel Andrews. The allegations are made in Federal Court documents filed by Paul Guerra, who was abruptly sacked by the Demons’ board in April after just seven months in the role, which had included an annual salary of $757,000 and bonuses. Former Melbourne CEO Paul Guerra has taken legal action against the club after being sacked in April. Joe Armao The claims of wage theft at the Demons could have broader implications for several other AFL clubs, after Guerra raised the matter with the chief people officer at the AFL, Sarah Fair, according to the statement of claim lodged last week. Melbourne Football Club has not yet had an opportunity to file a defence to Guerra’s statement of claim and his claims have not yet been tested in court. The Age is not suggesting Guerra’s allegations are true, only that they have been made in a court document.



“Ms Fair said that the AFL knows there is a problem across the AFL of clubs applying incorrect awards and the engagement of contractors who may have been employees, and that other clubs were also looking into this issue,” according to court documents. Within weeks of starting as chief executive, Guerra claims, he was told by general manager of partnerships Donna Kennett that her staff were also required to work on match days and were not compensated. “Ms Kennett told Mr Guerra words to the effect that this issue had been raised at the club in the past and had always been ‘shut down’,” according to the statement of claim. Guerra had then taken up the matter with human resources general manager Jess Vandelaak and then chief commercial officer Chris Kearon, who he claims both conceded it was an issue the club had ignored. Vandelaak also allegedly told Guerra that the club’s administrative staff, who include the executive and events teams, marketing, partnerships, retail and media, were all covered under the same award.



“Guerra became concerned that there was potentially a widespread underpayment problem at the club, specifically that there may have been other modern awards that applied to some administrative staff at the club,” it is alleged in court documents obtained by this masthead. Melbourne Football Club In February, Guerra appointed Sara Marriott as the club’s new chief people officer and requested she conduct a review to ensure all staff were classified under the correct award and paid their proper entitlements. However, Guerra claims his concerns were dismissed by several board members, who had insisted all staff payments had recently been found compliant by consultancy giant EY. Guerra claims on April 20 – about a week before he was sacked – he presented to the board the findings of Marriott’s review, which included the underpayment of six employees, while seven employees had been classified under the wrong award, and other roles needed to be urgently assessed.



“One of the employees who had been underpaid was a person with a disability, this underpayment went back over 10 years, and back-paying this employee may cause complications in relation to Commonwealth government payments that had been made to him,” the court documents state. The AFL engages a law firm that clubs can use for advice on awards and payment compliance, but compliance with awards is a matter for individual clubs. Guerra, who is a director at Racing Victoria, had also raised probity concerns about the board’s engagement of consultancy firm FMRS Advisory to assist with a plan to establish new headquarters at Caulfield Racecourse – in partnership with the Melbourne Racing Club. FMRS Advisory was founded by several former senior staffers under the Andrews government including Ben Foster, Jessie McCrone, Adam Sims and Lissie Ratcliff. Under its deal with the Demons, FMRS Advisory received its instructions and payment from the board of directors, rather than the chief executive. Guerra’s court document alleges that he complained about the arrangement with then president Brad Green.



“Guerra said he was uncomfortable with the fact that the board had engaged, and was directing, a contractor without his knowledge, control or visibility, in circumstances where Guerra was responsible for the club’s financial performance,” according to court documents. “Green said, in a dismissive tone, that Mr Guerra was not involved in the move to Caulfield Racecourse and therefore Mr Guerra did not need to be across it,” the documents state. FMRS declined to comment when contacted by The Age. According to the statement of claim, Guerra was sacked at a meeting on April 28, which lasted about five minutes. He was told that the board had lost confidence in his ability to lead the club. The Federal Court action launched by Guerra names the club and Demons president Steven Smith as respondents, and follows other legal claims against the Demons made in the same court by retired premiership defender Steven May and his partner Sachi Dade.



Sachi Dade and Steven May pictured in 2023. Getty Images Guerra’s lawyer, Alex Wolff from Baker McKenzie, states his client’s reports to the board about alleged underpayment of staff and the arrangement with FMRS Advisory fell under “his fundamental duties as chief executive, and were all critical and necessary to meet his obligations under the [employment] contract.” It is claimed in court documents that Guerra was entitled to protection under the Corporations Act and the Fair Work Act. Guerra, who declined to comment when contacted by this masthead on Sunday, is seeking more than $1 million in compensation from the club. A source with knowledge of the former Melbourne CEO’s interaction with the AFL, who declined to speak on the record while the matter was before the courts, told The Age the AFL had a different view on discussions involving Guerra.



They said no specific concerns were raised by Guerra about examples of underpayment at Melbourne or other clubs. Editor's pick Healthcare ‘People like me don’t have babies’: Inside the clinic helping addicted expectant mums The source said Guerra’s first meeting with the AFL in October-November was a general induction meeting for a new club CEO, and the second meeting was a meet and greet with the head of HR. The AFL declined to comment. A spokesman for the Melbourne Football Club also declined to comment. World.title: ‘We are simply fodder’: Fire rescue staff revolt against union boss
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian Fire Services ‘We are simply fodder’: Fire rescue staff revolt against union boss Kieran Rooney August 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

White-collar workers at Fire Rescue Victoria who have been waiting five years for a pay rise have urged the government to intervene as they argue union boss Peter Marshall is stalling their negotiations. A protracted dispute over the state’s firefighters will also rage for longer as the union moves to protect controversial veto clauses featured in two reports by the state’s corruption watchdog. United Firefighters Union boss Peter Marshall. Frustrated FRV staff have signed a petition calling on the agency and state government to bypass the union and put a deal directly to staff. Arsineh Houspian Corporate and technical staff at FRV, which includes roles in administration, support, legal and technology, have been due for a new enterprise agreement since 2021 but the United Firefighters Union has not put a deal to staff for a vote despite half a decade of negotiations. Frustrated staff have signed a petition, seen by The Age, calling on the agency and state government to bypass the union and put a deal directly to staff.



The delay has meant staff have not had a pay rise, including for inflation, since 2021. Two FRV staffers, speaking anonymously to avoid repercussions from the union, said they believed Marshall was reluctant to finalise the deal while he waited for the result of a separate pay dispute involving the state’s paid firefighters. That agreement, which has dragged on since 2022, is being considered by the Fair Work Commission, which typically would limit the United Firefighters Union’s ability to campaign on FRV worksites. But FRV corporate staff said that their EBA negotiations were acting as a loophole that allowed the union to keep using posters and perform other campaign activities that were not permitted for operational staff such as firefighters. One source said their pay deal was being dragged out as an unofficial bargaining tool for the firefighters.



“We are simply fodder for uniformed staff,” one said. Under typical arrangements, the union negotiates with FRV and ultimately decides when a pay deal is acceptable to put to the workforce for a vote. But this has not happened in five years of negotiations, prompting the petition from 160 staff. They asked the emergency services minister and FRV to make an offer directly to staff, bypassing the union entirely. A Fire Rescue Victoria spokesperson said they acknowledged the concerns raised by corporate and technical staff. “FRV understands that the prolonged industrial negotiations have been challenging for our corporate and technical workforce,” they said.



“We have bargained in good faith with the UFU for a replacement enterprise agreement since 2021 and have put forward seven offers, including our most recent in January 2026. FRV’s latest offer to the union was made on August 14 and the union advised it would respond by Friday. However on the union’s public website they describe the current offer as “not good enough”, sparking concerns employees will not get a chance to vote as requested. “FRV’s offer doesn’t come close to compensating you for the last six years,” the website says.

The offer includes an $8000 lump sump payment and back pay to January. Wages would increase by 6 per cent in 2026 and 3 per cent in 2027, 2028 and 2029.



Marshall has been contacted for comment. A Victorian government spokesperson said the negotiations had dragged on for too long. “The ball is now in the UFU’s court – FRV has made seven offers to resolve this agreement and deliver the pay rises workers deserve,” they said. Marshall’s protracted dispute over another pay deal for his firefighters will also drag out further after new federal legislation forced the Fair Work Commission to reconsider his arguments. It has also raised the prospect that he will be able to preserve some of the most contentious parts of the union’s current agreement, which featured in two IBAC reports and which the government has sought to unwind.



The firefighters’ pay deal in 2025 was sent to the Fair Work Commission after the union and the Victorian government were unable to reach an agreement. Marshall in 2022 sought annual pay rises for firefighters of 8.6 per cent but refused to budge on removing other conditions, including controversial “consult and agree” clauses inserted into Country Fire Authority and Metropolitan Fire Brigade pay deals before Fire Rescue Victoria was created. Related Article IBAC Champagne toasts, text boasts and treachery aplenty: Unpacking IBAC’s bombshell report Two separate IBAC reports into the United Firefighters Union have discussed these clauses and concerns that they effectively gave the union veto rights over key decisions made by the government and department. Operation Richmond, an investigation that started in 2018 and was released just last month, showed Marshall was particularly resistant to removing these clauses, despite them being opposed by the CFA, MFB and the late Jane Garrett, who was minister at the time.



As relations with Marshall soured, the Victorian government in 2025 sought to remove these clauses through the intractable bargaining process at the Fair Work Commission, backtracking on one of the key issues that had sparked the 2016 CFA pay deal saga in the first place. The union secretary then spent 12 months urging federal MPs on the crossbench to add new “no worse off” laws to the Fair Work Commission process, which he argues now mean his veto clauses cannot be removed. The legislation was passed in June and the change means the pay deal with Victorian firefighters, which is now four years overdue, has been delayed further. The Fair Work Commission had been deliberating on the matter since December. A FRV spokesperson said the timeline for these negotiations was beyond their control. They said recent federal changes meant the Fair Work Commission had invited them to make further submissions.



“Firefighters have made it clear they want their terms and conditions finalised as soon as possible, and FRV shares this goal,” they said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Chinese robots beat Usain Bolt’s 100m world record at Beijing games
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Beijing: A Chinese humanoid robot ran 100 metres in 9.39 seconds in a preliminary heat at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, faster than the men’s world record held by Jamaican sprinting great Usain Bolt.

Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre, won its heat on Saturday at the opening of the games’ second edition, organisers said.

The robot overtook smartphone maker Honor’s Lightning near the finish after falling behind early in the race. Lightning finished in 9.47 seconds, also faster than the 9.58-second record Bolt set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships in Berlin.

Loading

The two robots lacked Bolt’s flair, slamming straight into a thick mat designed to stop them in their tracks. Tiangong stumbled wildly into the sidelines, forcing onlookers to move out of the way. Lightning was carried away on a stretcher after collapsing to the ground.

World.title: Sydney Swans double-header: Women’s and men’s teams return to SCG after club’s week of scandal
World.content:
Embattled and understrength Sydney have beaten North Melbourne by 53 points in the Swans’ first game since the sexual assault allegations that rocked the AFL club.

Five players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon – were suspended on Wednesday for the rest of the season for “breaching club standards”.

The sanctions are separate to the police investigation into sexual assault allegations and the events at East Melbourne’s Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

Those events completely overshadowed a maiden AFLW-AFL double-header at the SCG, where, after Sydney’s women’s team beat Essendon by 24 points, the men won their game 17.21 (123) to 10.10 (70).

Sydney Swans fans get into the spirit at the SCG. Janie Barrett

After the AFLW team won in front of a record crowd of 16,672, a number of fans walked out – an action forecast by some as a reaction to the Pullman hotel storm.

Sydney’s men won what was effectively a dead-rubber in front of 30,058 fans – the club’s lowest AFL home crowd of the season.

Their previous low mark this year was 33,413; every other home crowd had breached 35,000, and with six attendances of 40,000 or more.

Sydney were already locked into second place on the ladder and will face either Brisbane or Hawthorn in a home qualifying final.

While the Swans will have next weekend off during the AFL wildcard round, in reality they face two more weeks in the spotlight before the finals.

No charges have been laid and AAP is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

Before the game, coach Dean Cox told Fox Footy he was confident the Swans had still prepared well despite the tough week.

Callum Mills of the Swans embraces Swans head coach Dean Cox. Getty Images

His undermanned Swans were clearly the better team and kept the Kangaroos at arm’s length.

Star Errol Gulden (41 disposals) stood tall along with skipper Callum Mills (26 disposals), Brodie Grundy (26 disposals, 27 hitouts), Braeden Campbell (20 disposals and two goals) and Tom Papley.

Mills and Gulden were in tears on the final siren, the emotions of the week spilling over as the crowd showed its vocal support for the club.

Boom recruit Charlie Curnow kicked 3.4 to finish his first season in Sydney with 69 goals, winning his third Coleman Medal as the AFL’s leading goalkicker.

Billy Cootee and Logan McDonald also kicked three goals each.

James Rowbottom, Harry Cunningham, Angus Sheldrick, Caiden Cleary and Tom Hanily were the five inclusions.

Callum Mills and Tom Papley of the Swans acknowledge the fans at the SCG. Getty Images

For North, former Swan Luke Parker (26 disposals) was busy along with Jy Simpkin (26) and Caleb Daniel (26), while Cam Zurhaar kicked two goals.

Sydney took the early ascendancy and shot out to a 39-point lead midway through the second quarter.

The Kangaroos responded late in the second term and in the third to claw the margin back to 21 at the final break.

Cootee kicked a settler at the start of the fourth quarter and from there, the Swans cruised.

World.title: Dutch F1 Grand Prix live: Piastri out to make history among the Zandvoort dunes
World.content:
Argentine President Javier Milei says he would push to bring Formula 1 back to Argentina, a race the nation has not hosted since 1998, and that he would personally drum up support in the coming weeks.

Milei said in a radio interview that he would attend the International Automobile Federation’s (FIA) Americas Congress, which is scheduled to take place between August 31 and September 2 in the capital.

Argentine President Javier Milei AP

The gathering, hosted by the Automovil Club Argentino, marks Argentina’s return to the international motorsport stage — the country has not hosted the event in nearly three decades.

“We are going to work to have Formula 1 back in Argentina again,” Milei said. “I’m also going to have a meeting with the people from the FIA.”

Gender equality From the Swans to Scots: Blaming the alleged victim means a harrowing truth can be avoided Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist “We are currently investigating the circumstances and preparing to commence legal proceedings against the club and potentially the individuals involved,” Manny Carbone, a partner at Carbone Lawyers, said. “Our clients are extremely traumatised and feel that their dignity and personal rights have been seriously violated by the events of Monday.” The Swans have denied there were any other club officials or staff members in the hotel room.



This masthead has previously reported that two sources familiar with the police investigation, but not authorised to speak publicly, confirmed drugs were involved in the early morning incident. However, both said the Swans teammates had denied being responsible for the drugs being there or taking them. World.title: Boning up on geography
World.content:
“Ah, Girilambone (C8),” effuses Bob Edgar of Moss Vale. “Nice choice, Janice Creenaune. I hope you have time for a delightful round trip via Gulargambone, Quambone and Billybingbone.”

“Letters to newspapers claiming the first sighting of magpies (C8) and blowflies are older than Granny,” reckons the canny Phil Kanaley of Glebe. “PG Wodehouse observed that ‘Nobody knows why, but editors have a weak spot for cuckoos, and anyone who hears the first one is pretty sure of an entree to their columns … what is known in my profession as ‘cuckoo-work’ … there is no market whatever for the second man who hears the cuckoo.’ At that time Granny was but a lass, not making her debut until 1947, but has since endured 79 summers of ornitho/entomo-logical encounters of the first kind.”

Edward Loong of Milsons Point reports that “not just one but three separate magpies were dive-bombing this morning adjacent to Wendy Whiteley’s Secret Garden at Lavender Bay, so I’m told by one of Wendy’s gardeners. He should know – being the target of all three. Unlike past years, I was spared – but fingers crossed for my morrows after.”

“The recent reference to the Edinburgh Writers’ Festival in the Herald reminded me of when we saw Terry Jones of Monty Python fame there many years ago,” says Nola Tucker of Kiama. “I bought his book and asked if he could dedicate it to my grandchildren. ‘Yes’, he replied, pen poised, ‘what are their names?’ ‘Just make it to the grandchildren as there are nine.’ Yes...’ very patiently ‘and what are their names?’ So I told him and still have the book with the nine grandchildren’s names neatly inscribed and his signature under them. Later on, we had a tenth grandchild, but I didn’t go back.”

Sometimes, a strict dress code (C8) can be a nice little earner. Here’s Paul Keys of Clouds Creek: “At the Hornsby Police Boys’ dance in the mid-’60s, the requirement was to wear socks, which could be purchased there. They also had some great bands playing.”

World.title: Swans’ AFLW team ride support for win; Magpies battling; Carlton on song
World.content:
Forward Nell Morris-Dalton has shown Carlton selectors that they made a worthwhile decision to salvage her AFLW career, as she dazzled in a 27-point victory over Adelaide.

Morris-Dalton booted three goals for the Blues (2-0) at Ikon Park to help last year’s preliminary finalists remain undefeated with a 7.8 (50) to 3.5 (23) win.

Carlton’s Nell Morris-Dalton. Getty Images

The performance comes after she was delisted by Collingwood at the end of last season and missed the initial cut for Carlton’s top-flight team after moving to their VFLW side.

But the 25-year-old was handed a lifeline when midfielder Maddy Guerin ruptured her ACL and on Sunday the injury replacement showed coach Mathew Buck that she deserves to be a mainstay.

World.title: Demons accused of wage theft and probity breaches by former CEO
World.content:
The former chief executive of the Melbourne Demons has claimed he was dismissed after raising concerns about widespread underpayment of administrative staff and complaining about the club’s use of a consultancy firm linked to former premier Daniel Andrews. The allegations are made in Federal Court documents filed by Paul Guerra, who was abruptly sacked by the Demons’ board in April after just seven months in the role, which had included an annual salary of $757,000 and bonuses. Former Melbourne CEO Paul Guerra has taken legal action against the club after being sacked in April. Joe Armao The claims of wage theft at the Demons could have broader implications for several other AFL clubs, after Guerra raised the matter with the chief people officer at the AFL, Sarah Fair, according to the statement of claim lodged last week. Melbourne Football Club has not yet had an opportunity to file a defence to Guerra’s statement of claim and his claims have not yet been tested in court. The Age is not suggesting Guerra’s allegations are true, only that they have been made in a court document.



“Ms Fair said that the AFL knows there is a problem across the AFL of clubs applying incorrect awards and the engagement of contractors who may have been employees, and that other clubs were also looking into this issue,” according to court documents. Within weeks of starting as chief executive, Guerra claims, he was told by general manager of partnerships Donna Kennett that her staff were also required to work on match days and were not compensated. “Ms Kennett told Mr Guerra words to the effect that this issue had been raised at the club in the past and had always been ‘shut down’,” according to the statement of claim. Guerra had then taken up the matter with human resources general manager Jess Vandelaak and then chief commercial officer Chris Kearon, who he claims both conceded it was an issue the club had ignored. Vandelaak also allegedly told Guerra that the club’s administrative staff, who include the executive and events teams, marketing, partnerships, retail and media, were all covered under the same award.



“Guerra became concerned that there was potentially a widespread underpayment problem at the club, specifically that there may have been other modern awards that applied to some administrative staff at the club,” it is alleged in court documents obtained by this masthead. Melbourne Football Club In February, Guerra appointed Sara Marriott as the club’s new chief people officer and requested she conduct a review to ensure all staff were classified under the correct award and paid their proper entitlements. However, Guerra claims his concerns were dismissed by several board members, who had insisted all staff payments had recently been found compliant by consultancy giant EY. Guerra claims on April 20 – about a week before he was sacked – he presented to the board the findings of Marriott’s review, which included the underpayment of six employees, while seven employees had been classified under the wrong award, and other roles needed to be urgently assessed.



“One of the employees who had been underpaid was a person with a disability, this underpayment went back over 10 years, and back-paying this employee may cause complications in relation to Commonwealth government payments that had been made to him,” the court documents state. The AFL engages a law firm that clubs can use for advice on awards and payment compliance, but compliance with awards is a matter for individual clubs. Guerra, who is a director at Racing Victoria, had also raised probity concerns about the board’s engagement of consultancy firm FMRS Advisory to assist with a plan to establish new headquarters at Caulfield Racecourse – in partnership with the Melbourne Racing Club. FMRS Advisory was founded by several former senior staffers under the Andrews government including Ben Foster, Jessie McCrone, Adam Sims and Lissie Ratcliff. Under its deal with the Demons, FMRS Advisory received its instructions and payment from the board of directors, rather than the chief executive. Guerra’s court document alleges that he complained about the arrangement with then president Brad Green.



“Guerra said he was uncomfortable with the fact that the board had engaged, and was directing, a contractor without his knowledge, control or visibility, in circumstances where Guerra was responsible for the club’s financial performance,” according to court documents. “Green said, in a dismissive tone, that Mr Guerra was not involved in the move to Caulfield Racecourse and therefore Mr Guerra did not need to be across it,” the documents state. FMRS declined to comment when contacted by The Age. According to the statement of claim, Guerra was sacked at a meeting on April 28, which lasted about five minutes. He was told that the board had lost confidence in his ability to lead the club. The Federal Court action launched by Guerra names the club and Demons president Steven Smith as respondents, and follows other legal claims against the Demons made in the same court by retired premiership defender Steven May and his partner Sachi Dade.



Sachi Dade and Steven May pictured in 2023. Getty Images Guerra’s lawyer, Alex Wolff from Baker McKenzie, states his client’s reports to the board about alleged underpayment of staff and the arrangement with FMRS Advisory fell under “his fundamental duties as chief executive, and were all critical and necessary to meet his obligations under the [employment] contract.” It is claimed in court documents that Guerra was entitled to protection under the Corporations Act and the Fair Work Act. Guerra, who declined to comment when contacted by this masthead on Sunday, is seeking more than $1 million in compensation from the club. A source with knowledge of the former Melbourne CEO’s interaction with the AFL, who declined to speak on the record while the matter was before the courts, told The Age the AFL had a different view on discussions involving Guerra.



They said no specific concerns were raised by Guerra about examples of underpayment at Melbourne or other clubs. Editor's pick Healthcare ‘People like me don’t have babies’: Inside the clinic helping addicted expectant mums The source said Guerra’s first meeting with the AFL in October-November was a general induction meeting for a new club CEO, and the second meeting was a meet and greet with the head of HR. The AFL declined to comment. A spokesman for the Melbourne Football Club also declined to comment.
